arXiv:2604.19592v2 [cs.LG] 04 Aug 2026

An Efficient Black-Box Reduction from Online Learning to Multicalibration, and a New Route to Φ\Phi-Regret Minimization

Gabriele Farina Affiliation: MIT EECS    Juan Carlos Perdomo Affiliation: MIT EECS Affiliation: New York University
Abstract

We give a Gordon-Greenwald-Marks (GGM) style black-box reduction from online learning to online multicalibration. Concretely, we show that to achieve high-dimensional multicalibration with respect to a class of functions ℋ\mathcal{H}, it suffices to combine any no-regret learner over ℋ\mathcal{H} with an expected variational inequality (EVI) solver. We also prove a converse statement showing that efficient multicalibration implies efficient EVI solving, highlighting how EVIs in multicalibration mirror the role of fixed points in the GGM result for Φ\Phi-regret.

This first set of results addresses the high-dimensional analogue of the open question in Garg, Jung, Reingold, and Roth (SODA ’24), showing that oracle-efficient online multicalibration with T\sqrt{T}-type guarantees is possible in full generality. Furthermore, our GGM-style reduction unifies the analyses of existing algorithms, transfers guarantees from online learning to multicalibration for challenging environments with delayed observations or censored outcomes, and yields the first efficient black-box reduction between online learning and multiclass omniprediction.

Our second main result is a fine-grained reduction from high-dimensional online multicalibration to (contextual) Φ\Phi-regret minimization. Together with our first result, this establishes a new route from external regret to Φ\Phi-regret that bypasses sophisticated fixed-point or semi-separation machinery, dramatically simplifies a result of Daskalakis, Farina, Fishelson, Pipis, and Schneider (STOC ’25) while improving rates, and yields new algorithms that are robust to richer deviation classes, such as those belonging to any reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

1 Introduction

Originally developed as a definition of algorithmic fairness, multicalibration has turned out to have interesting and important implications beyond its initial scope. Within learning theory, multicalibrated predictors are outcome indistinguishable; they constitute generative models that are computationally unfalsifiable [17]. Multicalibration also implies robustness to distribution shift [48] and loss minimization, not just for one loss, but for many losses simultaneously [33]. Within complexity theory, recent work has started to explore how multicalibration enables stronger versions of classical regularity lemmas, such as the Dense Model Theorem and the Hardcore Lemma [7, 45]. In game theory, notions of calibration are intimately tied to swap regret minimization and thus to correlated equilibria [26, 27, 47].

Despite this growing web of connections, the algorithmic understanding of how to achieve multicalibration remains rather fragmented. In the batch setting, the only known algorithms are boosting-style procedures that use polynomially more samples than necessary. In the online setting, where procedures enjoy worst-case guarantees and yield batch algorithms with optimal 𝒪⁡(1/ε2)\mathcal{O}(1/\varepsilon^{2}) sample complexity via online-to-batch reductions, we have a complicated patchwork of designs. Each algorithm targets a specific outcome type (e.g., binary) or hypothesis class (e.g., linear functions) and requires its own idiosyncratic and often lengthy analysis. In short, we lack a clean algorithmic template that works in full generality.

There is, however, a compelling precedent for a solution to this issue. Multicalibration is reminiscent of a different and older problem in online learning, namely Φ\Phi-regret minimization [36]. Both are parameterized by a family of functions: tests in the case of multicalibration, and a set Φ\Phi of strategy transformations ϕ:𝒵→𝒵\phi:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{Z} in the case of Φ\Phi-regret on a strategy set 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. Since the seminal result of [35] (henceforth abbreviated as Gordon-Greenwald-Marks or GGM), it is known that Φ\Phi-regret minimization can be efficiently reduced, black-box, to standard regret minimization over Φ\Phi, converting the outputs over Φ\Phi into strategies in 𝒵\mathcal{Z} by computing a fixed point of the transformations. Since 2008, this black-box reduction has been the standard approach for Φ\Phi-regret algorithms, and has led to a flurry of results for equilibrium computation (e.g., [19, 29, 13, 3] and references therein).

In light of the above, this paper is motivated by two questions.

  1. (Q1)

    Is there a Gordon-Greenwald-Marks-like reduction for online multicalibration? That is, can online multicalibration be black-box reduced to regret minimization, and if so, what nonlinear optimization primitive plays the role that fixed points play for Φ\Phi-regret?

  2. (Q2)

    How formal is the resemblance between multicalibrated forecasting and Φ\Phi-regret? Can one devise a more fine-grained connection between online ℋ\mathcal{H}-multicalibration and Φ\Phi-regret with ℋ\mathcal{H} scaling naturally with the complexity of Φ\Phi and recovering the well-known connection between strong calibration and swap regret in the limit?

We establish positive answers to both questions.

Our first contribution, addressing (Q1), is a Gordon-Greenwald-Marks-style theorem for online multicalibration. This resolves the high-dimensional version of one of the open questions in [30] regarding the existence of efficient oracle-based constructions for online multicalibration. Specifically, we show that online multicalibration can be obtained efficiently and in a black-box fashion with respect to any class ℋ\mathcal{H} and set of high-dimensional outcomes 𝒴\mathcal{Y} by combining external regret minimization over test functions in ℋ\mathcal{H} with the nonlinear optimization primitive of expected variational inequalities (EVIs). This black-box reduction is especially appealing in light of recent algorithmic progress on EVIs, demonstrating that they can be solved very efficiently [65]. Furthermore, we show that EVIs are not only sufficient but also necessary: contingent on an efficient oracle for online learning over ℋ\mathcal{H}, an efficient online multicalibrated forecasting algorithm exists if and only if one can efficiently solve EVIs defined by the test functions in ℋ\mathcal{H}. Importantly, our approach avoids binning or discretization arguments over the outcome space 𝒴\mathcal{Y} in order to preserve computational efficiency when outcomes yy are high-dimensional vectors.

Our reduction enables a technical transfer of ideas from the rich literature on online learning to the more recent area of multicalibration. Looking backward, we recover and dramatically simplify the proofs of prior online multicalibration algorithms. By leveraging recent advances in EVIs, these reinterpretations also yield stronger guarantees. Looking forward, we leverage our reduction to design new algorithms for previously unstudied versions of online multicalibration. In particular, we develop forecasting procedures with guarantees in challenging learning environments, such as settings with delayed feedback or censored observations, simply by swapping in the appropriate off-the-shelf regret minimizer. Given how online problems generate offline problems, these new algorithms also imply better batch algorithms via online-to-batch reductions.

Our second contribution, addressing (Q2), runs in the opposite direction: from forecasting to decision making. We show that an efficient no-Φ\Phi-regret algorithm can be constructed by first building an online forecaster for the losses that is multicalibrated with respect to a set of tests defined in terms of Φ\Phi, and then best responding. This result yields a substantially finer-grained reduction from decision making to forecasting than the folklore connection between swap regret and ℓ1\ell_{1}-multicalibration (e.g., [26]), and yields state-of-the-art Φ\Phi-regret algorithms for new domains.

Taken together, we show that our two main reductions provide an alternative path between external regret and Φ\Phi-regret to that established by [35]: Rather than optimizing directly over endomorphisms and then computing fixed points, one can route through multicalibration and EVIs. Recent work on Φ\Phi-regret minimization for expressive deviation classes has increasingly run into the limits of the GGM path: extending it to richer classes of deviations over general action sets 𝒵\mathcal{Z} has required increasingly elaborate machinery, including semi-separation oracles and careful relaxations of sets of endomorphisms [13]. Certain natural classes, such as deviations lying in any reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), have remained out of reach. Our multicalibration route provides a simplified technical approach that not only recovers prior results on linear and low-degree polynomial swap regret [13, 3, 66] but also establishes the first known no-Φ\Phi-regret algorithms for new settings, such as RKHSs.

1.1 Background: Online Forecasting and Decision-Making

The focus of our work is on understanding the algorithmic landscape and connections between online multicalibrated forecasting algorithms and online decision-making algorithms for Φ\Phi-regret. We start by defining both of these concepts formally.

While much of the literature has focused on one-dimensional, binned notions of multicalibration, in this paper we are interested in the high-dimensional, non-binned definition that has recently been studied (e.g., [15, Def. 1] and [18, Def. 3.2]). As we show in Section 3.4, this notion generalizes prior popular instantiations in the literature, such as ℓ1\ell_{1} notions of calibration (also known as expected calibration error or ECE), where errors are summed over a grid of discretized bins. See Remark 2 in Section 3.4 for further discussion.

Definition 1 (Online Multicalibration).

Consider the online protocol where at every time tt, Nature selects features xt∈𝒳x_{t}\in\mathcal{X}, and then the Learner produces a distribution 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} over forecasts pt∈𝒴⊂ℝdp_{t}\in\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} where 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is a compact, convex set. Lastly, Nature reveals the outcome yt∈𝒴y_{t}\in\mathcal{Y}.

An algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} guarantees online multicalibration with respect to a class ℋ⊆{𝒳×𝒴→ℝd}\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\}, if regardless of Nature’s choices of (xt,yt)(x_{t},y_{t}), the multicalibration error

MC-ErrT​(h)≔∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]\displaystyle\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h)\coloneqq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\Big]

grows sublinearly as a function of TT for all test functions h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H}. For brevity, we adopt the shorthand MC-ErrT≔suph∈ℋMC-ErrT​(h)\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}\coloneqq\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h).

Intuitively, the sequence of distributions 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} is multicalibrated if the expected errors, pt−ytp_{t}-y_{t}, are uncorrelated with any function in the class ℋ\mathcal{H}. Here, we stated the definition without absolute values, since it allows for finer-grained results. However, one can always recover the absolute values by requiring ℋ\mathcal{H} to be symmetric, meaning that for any h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H}, −h-h is also in the class.

Next, we define Φ\Phi-regret. We opt to present the slightly more permissive definition described by [64], which enables the Learner to output distributions over points in 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at every round. This definition preserves connections between Φ\Phi-regret and Φ\Phi-equilibria, but enables efficient algorithmic paths that the original definition of [36] precluded when Φ\Phi contains nonlinear functions.11 1 Conversely, when all transformations in Φ\Phi are linear, the expectation can be pushed through the deviation, and any Φ\Phi-regret minimizer in the more permissive sense of Definition 2 can be coalesced into the less permissive definition in which a single point (the expectation of μt\mu_{t}) is output.

Definition 2 (Φ\Phi-Regret Minimization).

Fix a set of deviations Φ⊆{𝒵→𝒵}\Phi\subseteq\{\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{Z}\} where 𝒵⊂ℝd\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is a compact, convex set of actions. Consider the online protocol in which, at each time tt, the Learner selects a distribution μt\mu_{t} over actions in 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, and then Nature reveals a loss vector ℓt∈ℝd\ell_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} from some set ℒ\mathcal{L}. An algorithm guarantees no-Φ\Phi-regret if it selects μt\mu_{t} such that no matter Nature’s choices of ℓt\ell_{t}

Φ​-RegretT​(ϕ)≔∑t=1T𝔼zt∼μt​[ℓt⊤​zt−ℓt⊤​ϕ​(zt)]\Phi\textup{-Regret}_{T}(\phi)\coloneqq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{z_{t}\sim\mu_{t}}\Big[\ell_{t}^{\top}z_{t}-\ell_{t}^{\top}\phi(z_{t})\Big]

grows sublinearly as a function of TT for all transformations ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi. We adopt the shorthand RegretT≔supϕ∈ΦRegretT​(ϕ)\textrm{Regret}_{T}\coloneqq\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\textrm{Regret}_{T}(\phi).

When Φ\Phi is the set of all constant functions, Φ\Phi-regret reduces to standard (also known as external) regret. At the opposite extreme, when Φ\Phi is the set of all functions from 𝒵\mathcal{Z} to 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, it captures full swap regret. Swap regret is, however, known to be hard to minimize over general convex sets 𝒵\mathcal{Z} [14], motivating a line of work proposing algorithms and definitions that guarantee low regret with respect to increasingly rich, yet tractable classes of deviations (e.g., [51, 21, 3, 19, 50, 29] and references therein).

The GGM paradigm.

The celebrated result of [35] established that Φ\Phi-regret minimization can be reduced, in a black-box fashion, to external regret minimization over the class Φ\Phi. The nonlinear optimization primitive enabling this reduction is the computation of expected fixed points (EFPs),22 2 Technically, [35] uses fixed points, but their result goes through directly for our more permissive definition of Φ\Phi-regret if one instead uses expected fixed points, which are easier to compute. See [64] for further discussion. which solve the following problem.

Given an endomorphism ϕ:𝒵→𝒵\phi:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{Z} and ε>0\varepsilon>0, find a polynomially-supported discrete distribution μ\mu over 𝒵\mathcal{Z} such that

‖𝔼x∼μ​[ϕ⁡(x)−x]‖2≤ε.\displaystyle\big\|\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu}[\phi(x)-x]\big\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon.

With that primitive, the following result can be shown.

Theorem 1 ([35], Informal).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be any external regret minimizer for the set of transformations Φ\Phi. Then, given the ability to efficiently solve expected fixed points for any ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi, 𝒜\mathcal{A} can be efficiently converted in a black-box fashion into an efficient online algorithm 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime} that guarantees no-Φ\Phi-regret over 𝒵\mathcal{Z}.

This reduction has been the de facto algorithmic template for Φ\Phi-regret minimization and its related equilibrium notions. As an example, the classical reduction from swap regret to external regret of [6], and from internal regret to external regret of [61], are particular instantiations of this framework.33 3 In [6], the expected fixed point computation subproblem is solved by computing the stationary distribution of a Markov chain. Furthermore, as pointed out by [41], the use of expected fixed points is not accidental. Any efficient algorithm for no-Φ\Phi-regret implies an efficient algorithm for solving expected fixed points for any ϕ\phi.

1.2 Contributions and Techniques

A GGM-Style Reduction for Online Multicalibration.

Our first result establishes an analogous result to that of [35], but this time between online learning and multicalibration, rather than Φ\Phi-regret. We show that multicalibration with respect to a set ℋ\mathcal{H} can be efficiently reduced, in a black-box fashion, to online learning over the class ℋ\mathcal{H} using a nonlinear optimization tool called an expected variational inequality (EVI).

EVIs have appeared in different literatures with different names, including “outgoing minimax problems” [24], “accuracy certificates” [52], or “negative correlation search” [59]. Given a function S:𝒴→ℝdS:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} from a set 𝒴⊂ℝd\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and error ε>0\varepsilon>0, the solution to the corresponding EVI is a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} over 𝒴\mathcal{Y} such that

𝔼p∼𝒟​[S​(p)⊤​(y−p)]≤ε∀y∈𝒴.\mathbb{E}_{p\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[S(p)^{\top}(y-p)\Big]\leq\varepsilon\qquad\forall y\in\mathcal{Y}. (EVI)

As we recall in Fact 1 below, EVIs can be solved efficiently, with runtime scaling as log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon) as a function of the desired precision ε\varepsilon for any convex and compact set 𝒴\mathcal{Y} and general (nonmonotone, or even discontinuous) operator SS, under minimal assumptions.

The following theorem summarizes our first main result.

Theorem 2 (Informal).

The following statements are true for a general high-dimensional outcome space 𝒴⊆ℝd\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} and function class ℋ⊆{𝒳×𝒴→ℝd}\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\}.

  • •

    (Online Learning and EVI →\to Multicalibration) Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be any online optimization algorithm over the class ℋ\mathcal{H} with external regret bounded by RegretT\textrm{Regret}_{T}. When paired with an EVI solver, we obtain an online algorithm whose multicalibration error with respect to ℋ\mathcal{H} is at most RegretT\textrm{Regret}_{T}.

  • •

    (Multicalibration →\to EVI) Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be any algorithm that efficiently guarantees online multicalibration with respect to ℋ\mathcal{H}, then 𝒜\mathcal{A} can be black-box converted into an efficient algorithm for solving EVIs over ℋ\mathcal{H}.

The reduction and its proof fit in a few lines (see Theorem 4), and are fully black-box. It makes no assumptions on ℋ\mathcal{H}, works for any convex compact 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, does not rely on binning arguments, and is hence amenable to general high-dimensional problems. As an immediate consequence, it resolves the high-dimensional version of one of the open questions in [30], who asked whether oracle-efficient multicalibration algorithms with T\sqrt{T} rates exist.

As with the celebrated GGM theorem for Φ\Phi-regret, this general reduction has several implications for the algorithmic landscape of online multicalibration. To start, we show how previous algorithms with lengthy, elaborate proofs can be recovered and improved by selecting different online learning algorithms and EVI solvers in the reduction. These include the K29 algorithm, as proposed in [62] and extended in [16, 20], and the unbiased prediction algorithm of [53]. Using the online learning algorithm from [10] as the online learning, a special case of our reduction yields an algorithm which achieves ℓ1\ell_{1} or ECE calibration with respect to vector-valued outcomes at the optimal 𝒪⁡(Td+1d+2)\mathcal{O}(T^{\frac{d+1}{d+2}}) rate (Section 3.4).

Beyond its conceptual simplicity and ability to recover known results, we also show how to use our reduction to derive simple algorithms for more complex multicalibrated forecasting tasks. In particular, by drawing on the well-developed literature on online learning, we design the first online multicalibration algorithms that succeed even in the face of delayed or censored outcomes. All of these follow as simple corollaries of Theorem 4.

Furthermore, our contributions for online multicalibration flow through to yield improved algorithms for solution concepts that are implications of multicalibration, such as online omniprediction or outcome indistinguishability. In particular, our results yield an efficient black-box reduction for online multiclass omniprediction for general loss functions and hypothesis classes.

An Alternative Path to Φ\Phi-regret.

Our second main contribution runs in the opposite direction, from forecasting to decision-making.

Theorem 3 (Informal).

Let σ⁡(p)∈arg⁡minz∈𝒵​p⊤​z\sigma(p)\in\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\;p^{\top}z denote the best-response map. For every deviation ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi, define the test function hϕ​(p)≔σ⁡(p)−ϕ⁡(σ⁡(p))h_{\phi}(p)\coloneqq\sigma(p)-\phi(\sigma(p)), and let ℋΦ≔{hϕ:ϕ∈Φ}\mathcal{H}_{\Phi}\coloneqq\{h_{\phi}:\phi\in\Phi\}. Then, any online forecaster of the losses ℓt\ell_{t} that is multicalibrated with respect to the class ℋΦ\mathcal{H}_{\Phi} can be black-box converted to an efficient no-Φ\Phi-regret algorithm by simply best-responding to the forecasts.

This theorem yields a substantially finer-grained reduction from decision-making to forecasting than the folklore connection between the demanding notion of swap regret and the demanding notion of ℓ1\ell_{1}-calibration. As discussed previously, swap regret minimization is inefficient on general sets (e.g., [14]), which begs the question: What is the richest class of deviations Φ\Phi that one can handle? We address that question by establishing a more precise connection between deviations ϕ\phi and multicalibration tests hϕh_{\phi}, thus obtaining reductions in which the required multicalibration class scales naturally with the complexity of Φ\Phi. This fine-grained reduction recovers the classical connection between strong calibration and swap regret only in the limit when Φ\Phi is the set of all deviations.

Together with the previous result, this theorem gives an alternative to the reduction of [35] (see Figure 1). This route, grounded in forecasting and EVIs rather than fixed points, has features that make it appealing when the set of deviations Φ\Phi is large. Perhaps most importantly, unlike the GGM framework, this route does not require an understanding of the geometry of endomorphisms of the action space, dispensing with much of the technical complexity in recent extensions. We highlight that this leads to a substantially different construction for the recent STOC paper on linear swap regret [13]: we improve the rates, completely avoid the semiseparation machinery needed there to handle endomorphisms, and even obtain an extension to general RKHS deviation classes, yielding the first algorithm for that setting. Furthermore, we highlight that these results hold not just for Φ\Phi-regret, but also for contextual versions of Φ\Phi-regret as we explain in Section 2.

We close this section by noting that online linear optimization is a special case of Φ\Phi-regret minimization. Online linear optimization and Φ\Phi-regret minimization are equivalent when the set Φ\Phi only contains a convex set of constant transformations. Therefore, our results show that given a general algorithm for online multicalibration, one can build a general algorithm for online linear optimization, and vice versa, highlighting a computational equivalence between the two problems.

1.3 Related Work

Our work lies at the intersection of various areas. Here, we briefly outline how our results build on and contribute to the most closely related work in each.

Multicalibration.

Multicalibration was introduced in the batch setting by [43] as a definition of algorithmic fairness. As discussed previously, multicalibration has a wide range of interesting consequences, including outcome indistinguishability [17], omniprediction [33, 32, 16, 55], and universal adaptability [48]. Within complexity theory, it implies stronger versions of the Dense Model theorem, the Hardcore Lemma, and other pseudorandomness notions [18, 8, 7, 45].

Batch notions of multicalibration are achievable via boosting algorithms that repeatedly call a weak agnostic learning oracle. These procedures are sample inefficient by at least a quadratic factor [43]. In the online setting, where T\sqrt{T} regret algorithms imply sample-efficient batch procedures, algorithms date back at least to [62] and [25], with increased activity following the work by [39]. In the setting where outcomes are high-dimensional, algorithms are known for special cases such as when ℋ\mathcal{H} is any finite set of functions [53], or any vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert space [20].

Prior work has established reductions between multicalibration and regret minimization in specific settings. [40] show a reduction for the restricted case of multiclass outcomes. However, their result is both white-box and exponential-time since it relies on constructing an ε\varepsilon-net of the dd-dimensional simplex. [30] prove a reduction between swap multicalibration and online regression that works for the specific case of binary outcomes and yields ω⁡(T)\omega(\sqrt{T}) rates. They leave as their main open question how to achieve an efficient black-box reduction for (vanilla) online multicalibration that achieves T\sqrt{T} rates, a problem we solve not just for binary yy but for general high-dimensional outcomes. [31] show a similar reduction for the case of binary outcomes and ℓ1\ell_{1} multicalibration, a distinct notion from ours for which T\sqrt{T} rates are unachievable [12]. Most recently, [44] showed an oracle-efficient reduction from ℓp\ell_{p} calibration to weak agnostic learning solving the open question in [30] for the special case of binary outcomes. Their construction differs from ours in at least two important directions. First, their results rely on discretization and binning arguments. They are limited to binary outcomes and do not apply to general high-dimensional or real-valued outcomes 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. Second, their reduction uses multiple learners which are trained conditionally, unlike our reduction which only uses one (Algorithm 1).

Φ\Phi-Regret Minimization.

Virtually all algorithms for Φ\Phi-regret minimization rely, either directly or indirectly, on the GGM result that uses fixed points. This is true of the celebrated no-swap-regret algorithm for normal-form games of [6] and the no-internal-regret for normal-form games of [61]. Both are specific instantiations of the general reduction in [35]. GGM also applies to several important algorithms for extensive-form games, including constructions of efficient algorithms for extensive-form correlated, extensive-form coarse-correlated equilibria, and linear correlated equilibria [51, 19, 22]. In contemporary work, the GGM framework has been pushed to its limits. Recent work has resorted to highly sophisticated semi-separation arguments to achieve regret minimization via the GGM path with respect to ever-increasing sets of transformations Φ\Phi and general convex action sets [13, 66, 3]. Our alternative path is simpler and achieves rates that match or improve upon those discussed here.

EVIs and Convex Sets.

Lastly, our reductions heavily rely on the ability to solve expected variational inequalities, as defined in (EVI). Recent work has developed efficient polynomial-time algorithms for solving these for any bounded operator SS on convex sets 𝒵\mathcal{Z} given an oracle (an algorithm that tests membership, performs separation, or linear optimization over 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, all of which are known to be polynomial-time-reducible to each other under minimal regularity conditions [38, 37]) for 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. In particular, the only assumption that we make is that 𝒵\mathcal{Z} has been shifted and scaled appropriately so that the following condition holds.

Definition 3 (Well-bounded set).

We say that a convex and compact set 𝒵⊆ℝd\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} is well-bounded if it contains in its relative interior a unit-radius Euclidean ball, and 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is contained in a Euclidean ball of radius poly⁡(d)\mathrm{poly}(d) centered in the origin.

For any convex body 𝒵\mathcal{Z} for which radii r,R>0r,R>0 are known such that a ball of radius rr is contained in the interior of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} and 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is contained in the ball of radius RR centered in the origin, a transformation that makes 𝒵\mathcal{Z} well-bounded can be computed in time polynomial in log⁡(R/r)\log(R/r) using a polynomial number of oracle calls [38, Corollary 4.6.8]. The assumption of well-boundedness allows us to ignore the terms log⁡(R/r)\log(R/r), and simply replace them with poly⁡(d)\mathrm{poly}(d). Under well-boundedness assumptions, we recall the following result.

Fact 1 ([65]).

Given a well-bounded convex compact set 𝒵⊆ℝd\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} and an operator S:𝒵→ℝdS:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} such that supz∈𝒵‖S⁡(z)‖≤B\sup_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\|S(z)\|\leq B, there exists an efficient algorithm that solves the EVI problem over SS to error ε\varepsilon in 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(d,log⁡(B/ε),eval⁡(S)))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(d,\log(B/\varepsilon),\mathrm{eval}(S))) time, where eval⁡(S)\mathrm{eval}(S) is an upper bound on the time it takes to evaluate SS. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, the algorithm returns a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} such that ∀y∈𝒵\forall y\in\mathcal{Z},

𝔼p∼𝒟​[S​(p)⊤​(y−p)]≤ε,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[S(p)^{\top}(y-p)\Big]\leq\varepsilon,

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} has positive mass on at most 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(d,log⁡(B/ε)))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(d,\log(B/\varepsilon))) points.

This fact, shown in [65], uses a generalization of the ellipsoid-against-hope algorithm [22, 56, 46]. However, slower algorithms that avoid the ellipsoid method also exist. For example, one can always solve EVIs via online linear optimization over 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. This regret minimization procedure solves EVIs to error ε\varepsilon in OPEN𝒪⁡(poly⁡(d,B,time⁡(S))/ε2))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(d,B,\mathrm{time}(S))/\varepsilon^{2})) time and returns a distribution with support size 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(d,B))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(d,B)). Both algorithmic paths (the fast one of Fact 1 and the slower approach based on regret minimization) are essentially enabled by algorithmic constructions of the minimax theorem (see also [23] for a high-level discussion).

Blackwell Approachability.

Dating back (at least) to the work of [28], tools from Blackwell approachability [5] have been repeatedly used as subroutines to build online algorithms for calibration and multicalibration via tailored, problem-specific constructions. For the restricted case of 1-dimensional outcomes, [54, 55, 59] encode finitely many discretized (multi)calibration conditions as the coordinates of a vector-valued game and employ approachability to achieve online calibration. Going beyond finite constraints, [58] defines a measure over calibration constraints and uses infinite-dimensional approachability for weighted average of these constraints. These results, however, rely on binning and discretization arguments, and are hence not computationally efficient in high-dimensional settings. Furthermore, the Blackwell game usually has one payoff for each test, putting into question this route for richer test sets such as the RKHS tests we discuss in Section 3.1 and use in Section 4. In contrast, our reductions are computationally efficient even for vector-valued outcomes, and can guarantee multicalibration with respect to every function in an infinitely large class of tests (see the example in Section 2.1).

On a more conceptual level, our work establishes black-box reductions between online linear optimization (OLO is a special case of Φ\Phi-regret) and online high-dimensional multicalibration, highlighting a new computational equivalence between these problems. This result complements prior work by [1] who established an equivalence between Blackwell approachability and online linear optimization. Tying both sets of results together, our EVI-based reductions highlight how Blackwell approachability is not just a bespoke tool for the design of specific calibration algorithms, but rather computationally equivalent to the most general version of this class of problems (that is, online high-dimensional multi-calibration).

2 A GGM-Like Theorem for Multicalibration, and Finer-Grained Connections between Decision-Making and Forecasting

In this section, we state our first result showing that multicalibration can be black-box reduced to online learning, and that Φ\Phi-regret minimization can be black-box reduced to multicalibration. These reductions enable a number of algorithmic corollaries, which we discuss in Sections 3 and 4.

2.1 Reducing Multicalibration to Online Learning via EVIs

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a set of features, 𝒴⊆ℝd\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact, convex set of outcomes, and ℋ⊆{𝒳×𝒴→ℝd}\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\} be a set of bounded test functions. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be any no-regret learner for ℋ\mathcal{H}, that is, an algorithm that selects hth_{t}, observes linear losses ftf_{t}, and guarantees sublinear external regret

RegretT​(h)≔∑t=1Tft​(ht)−ft​(h)\displaystyle\textrm{Regret}_{T}(h)\coloneqq\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(h_{t})-f_{t}(h) (2)

with respect to any h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H}. We again let RegretT=suph∈ℋRegretT​(h)\textrm{Regret}_{T}=\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\textrm{Regret}_{T}(h).

Algorithm 1 shows how 𝒜\mathcal{A} can be black-box converted into an online multicalibration procedure over ℋ\mathcal{H}. The idea is simple. We use 𝒜\mathcal{A} to determine which test function in ℋ\mathcal{H} to prioritize in each round. Given the current context xtx_{t}, and the test hth_{t} selected by 𝒜\mathcal{A}, we convert hth_{t} into a distribution 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} over the forecasts pt∼𝒟tp_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t} by solving the EVI corresponding to ht​(xt,⋅)h_{t}(x_{t},\cdot), as shown in (1); we recall that EVIs can be solved efficiently under minimal assumptions (see Fact 1). Finally, upon receiving the actual outcome yt∈𝒴y_{t}\in\mathcal{Y} from the environment, we supply the loss ft​(h)f_{t}(h) (which is always linear in hh) back to the no-regret algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

The following theorem is our first main result establishing the correctness of this reduction.

Theorem 4.

Fix h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} and let RegretT​(h)\textrm{Regret}_{T}(h) denote the regret cumulated by the external regret minimizer 𝒜\mathcal{A} (as in Equation 2) where ftf_{t} are defined as in Algorithm 1 and EVIT≔∑t=1Tεt\mathrm{EVI}_{T}\coloneqq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\varepsilon_{t} is the sum of the EVI errors from Equation 1, then the sequence of distributions 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} output by the Learner in Algorithm 1 satisfy the following inequality,

MC-ErrT​(h)≤RegretT​(h)+EVIT.\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h)\leq\textrm{Regret}_{T}(h)+\mathrm{EVI}_{T}.
Proof.

The key is that the EVI property guarantees that

0≤εt−𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[ht​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)].0\leq\varepsilon_{t}-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h_{t}(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\Big].

Therefore,

∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\Big] ≤∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]−𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[ht​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]+εt\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\Big]-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h_{t}(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\Big]+\varepsilon_{t}
=(∑t=1Tft​(ht)−ft​(h))+∑t=1Tεt\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(h_{t})-f_{t}(h)\right)+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\varepsilon_{t}
=RegretT​(h)+EVIT.∎\displaystyle=\textrm{Regret}_{T}(h)+\mathrm{EVI}_{T}.\qed

Since EVIT\textrm{EVI}_{T} can always be chosen to be less than RegretT\textrm{Regret}_{T}, we get that if 𝒜\mathcal{A} guarantees that RegretT\textrm{Regret}_{T} is o⁡(T)o(T), then the multicalibration error with respect to ℋ\mathcal{H} is also o⁡(T)o(T).

Before we discuss the necessity of EVIs, we briefly pause to illustrate how Theorem 4 can be used to easily design online multicalibration algorithms in two important settings. We keep the discussion short and informal to focus on the overarching idea and defer a detailed presentation of (stronger versions of) these results to Section 3.

Multicalibration with respect to finite sets.

To start, suppose we would like to produce forecasts of high-dimensional outcomes y∈𝒴⊂ℝdy\in\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} that are multicalibrated with respect to all functions in the convex hull of a finite set of tests ℋ\mathcal{H}. That is, ℋ=conv⁡{h(1),…,h(n)}\mathcal{H}=\co\{h^{(1)},\dots,h^{(n)}\} for some n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. We assume that evaluating each h(i)h^{(i)} incurs a cost polynomial in the dimension dd, and that |h(i)​(x,p)⊤​(y−p)|≤1|h^{(i)}(x,p)^{\top}(y-p)|\leq 1 for all i∈[n]i\in[n], x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, and y,p∈𝒴y,p\in\mathcal{Y}.

Applying Algorithm 1 using Hedge as the no-regret algorithm over ℋ\mathcal{H} yields a forecaster for 𝒴\mathcal{Y} that is multicalibrated with respect to each h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H}, that runs in time 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n​d)​log⁡t)\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(nd)\log t) at every iteration tt, and achieves multicalibration error

MC-ErrT​(h)≤𝒪⁡(T​log⁡n).\displaystyle\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h)\leq\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T\log n}). (3)

In more detail, at every time tt, Hedge outputs a function hth_{t} which is a convex combination of the functions in ℋ\mathcal{H}, ht=λt(1)​h(1)+⋯+λt(n)​h(n)∈ℋh_{t}=\lambda^{(1)}_{t}h^{(1)}+\dots+\lambda^{(n)}_{t}h^{(n)}\in\mathcal{H}. Evaluating such hth_{t} incurs a cost 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n​d)).\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(nd)). Using the EVI algorithm of [65], we can then solve each EVI induced by ht​(xt,⋅)h_{t}(x_{t},\cdot) to precision 1/t1/t in time 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n​d)​log⁡t)\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(nd)\log t), yielding the distribution 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} with support size 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(d)​log⁡t)\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(d)\log t) and EVIT=∑t=1T1/t≤𝒪⁡(log⁡(T))\textrm{EVI}_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}1/t\leq\mathcal{O}(\log(T)).

Upon observing the realized yt∈𝒴y_{t}\in\mathcal{Y}, we can then update the convex combination coefficients λt,1,…,λt,n\lambda_{t,1},\dots,\lambda_{t,n} according to the Hedge algorithm. In particular, in light of the definition of ftf_{t} in Algorithm 1, each coefficient is updated according to

λt+1(i)∝λt(i)⋅exp⁡{η​𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h(i)​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]}\lambda^{(i)}_{t+1}\propto\lambda^{(i)}_{t}\cdot\exp\bigg\{\eta\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h^{(i)}(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\Big]\bigg\}

for some appropriate learning rate η>0\eta>0. Since 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} has support 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(d)​log⁡t)\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(d)\log t), the update can be carried out in time 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n​d)​log⁡t)\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(nd)\log t). Invoking Theorem 4 with the known regret bound of Hedge, we obtain the bound in Equation 3.

Multicalibration with respect to infinitely many tests.

The reduction we devised is useful well beyond (convex hulls of) discrete tests. It applies just as easily to infinite, structured families of test functions, such as all functions that lie in the unit ball of a vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This setting includes, for example, multicalibration with respect to all low-degree polynomials, decision trees, or in the case where 𝒴=[0,1]\mathcal{Y}=[0,1], all Lipschitz continuous functions of the forecast pp [16, 63] (this last case is known as smooth calibration [47]).

To keep the example concrete, suppose we are interested in building an online forecaster of high-dimensional outcomes that is multicalibrated with respect to all polynomials in (x,p)(x,p) of degree up to r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N}. Here, x∈𝒳⊆ℝmx\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} and p∈𝒴⊆ℝdp\in\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}. Specifically, consider the feature map φ⁡(x,p)\varphi(x,p) listing all monomials in (x,p)(x,p) of degree up to rr. Every vector-valued function h⁡(x,p)h(x,p) whose iith coordinate is any polynomial in (x,p)(x,p) of degree up to rr can be written as a linear function of φ⁡(x,p)\varphi(x,p). That is, h⁡(x,p)=M​φ​(x,p)h(x,p)=M\varphi(x,p). Assuming a bound on the norm of the coefficients of matrices MM, we can guarantee multicalibration with respect to the set of functions

ℋ≔{(x,p)↦M​φ​(x,p):‖M‖F≤1}.\mathcal{H}\coloneqq\{(x,p)\mapsto M\varphi(x,p):\|M\|_{F}\leq 1\}.

In this case, the set of test functions is indexed by matrices MM which span a unit ball. We can then invoke Algorithm 1 using a no-regret learner 𝒜\mathcal{A} for online optimization over the ℓ2\ell_{2} ball (for example, projected gradient descent), and directly obtain an efficient T\sqrt{T} multicalibrated forecaster for all low-degree polynomial functions hh since the losses in Algorithm 1, ft​(h)=ft​(M)f_{t}(h)=f_{t}(M), remain linear in MM. We will return to this construction in Sections 3 and 4, where we illustrate how it extends well beyond low-degree polynomials.

2.1.1 The Necessity of EVIs: Reducing EVIs to Online Multicalibration

The previous theorem shows that one can construct a ℋ\mathcal{H}-multicalibrated forecaster from a no-regret learner over ℋ\mathcal{H}, provided that EVIs can be solved efficiently. Thus, EVIs are sufficient to construct multicalibrated forecasters. A natural question, however, is whether they are also the “right” primitive for this problem. In this subsection, we point out that EVIs are necessary as well, in the sense that the existence of an efficient ℋ\mathcal{H}-multicalibrated forecaster automatically implies the existence of an efficient EVI solver over functions in ℋ\mathcal{H}. In this respect, our result parallels the reduction of [35] between external regret and Φ\Phi-regret, where (expected) fixed points are sufficient and necessary in the analogous sense [41].

To show necessity, suppose that we have an ℋ\mathcal{H}-multicalibrated forecaster, that is, an algorithm that produces distributions 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} such that for any h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} and arbitrary sequence {(xt,yt)}t=1T\{(x_{t},y_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T},

1T​∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]≤1T​MC-ErrT\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\Big]\leq\frac{1}{T}\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}

where MC-ErrT\textrm{MC-Err}_{T} is o⁡(T)o(T). We show that the above algorithm can be turned into an algorithm for solving EVIs defined in terms of any xx and hh to any error ε>0\varepsilon>0:

𝔼p∼𝒟​[h​(x,p)⊤​(y−p)]≤ε∀y∈𝒴.\mathbb{E}_{p\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[h(x,p)^{\top}(y-p)\Big]\leq\varepsilon\qquad\forall y\in\mathcal{Y}.

To see this, consider the scenario in which Nature picks xt=xx_{t}=x at all times. Let 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} be the distribution returned by the ℋ\mathcal{H}-calibrated forecaster. We will let the yty_{t} be a best response

yt≔arg​maxy^∈𝒴⁡y^⊤​[𝔼pt∼𝒟t​h​(x,pt)].\displaystyle y_{t}\coloneqq\argmax_{\hat{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}\hat{y}^{\top}\left[\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}h(x,p_{t})\right].

Then, we have that for any fixed y⋆∈𝒴y_{\star}\in\mathcal{Y}

1T​MC-ErrT\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\textrm{MC-Err}_{T} ≥1T​∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(x,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]≥1T​∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(x,pt)⊤​(y⋆−pt)].\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h(x,p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\Big]\geq\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h(x,p_{t})^{\top}(y_{\star}-p_{t})\Big].

As T→∞T\to\infty, MC-ErrT/T→0\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}/T\to 0 and the uniform mixture 𝒟\mathcal{D} over 𝒟1,…,𝒟T\mathcal{D}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{D}_{T} is a solution to the EVI defined by h⁡(x,⋅)h(x,\cdot).

2.2 Φ\Phi-Regret Minimization from Online Multicalibration

In this subsection, we provide a fine-grained reduction between Φ\Phi-regret minimization and multicalibrated forecasting. The connection between swap regret (the special case where Φ\Phi contains all endomorphisms on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}) and best responses to ℓ1\ell_{1}-calibrated forecasters is by now folklore, dating at least to [26]. However, recent work has shown that swap regret is hard to minimize efficiently beyond the case where 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is the simplex, motivating the study of more structured deviation classes Φ\Phi [14]. Furthermore, ℓ1\ell_{1} notions of calibration are strictly harder to achieve [12], motivating the question of whether they are strictly necessary to guarantee low regret.

Our main contribution here establishes that less demanding notions of Φ\Phi-regret are efficiently achievable via correspondingly less demanding notions of multicalibration, making this celebrated connection between prediction and decision-making more precise. Specifically, if the goal is to guarantee low regret against a set of deviations Φ\Phi, we show that it suffices to best respond to forecasts of the losses that are multicalibrated with respect to the following set of tests:

ℋΦ≔{(x,p)↦σ⁡(p)−ϕ⁡(σ⁡(p)):ϕ∈Φ},σ⁡(p)≔arg​minz∈𝒵⁡p⊤​z.\mathcal{H}_{\Phi}\coloneqq\{(x,p)\mapsto\sigma(p)-\phi(\sigma(p)):\phi\in\Phi\},\qquad\sigma(p)\coloneqq\argmin_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}p^{\top}z. (4)

We assume that ties in the best response problem on the right are broken deterministically according to some arbitrary scheme, so that σ\sigma is a function. Quite intuitively, as the set of deviations Φ\Phi against which regret is minimized grows, so grows the corresponding set ℋΦ\mathcal{H}_{\Phi} of multicalibration tests. We discuss in Section 4 how this fine-grained reduction enables efficient guarantees for rich but structured families of deviations, representing a step change in the simplicity of the algorithms for achieving no-Φ\Phi-regret against large classes of deviations Φ\Phi, and extending naturally to settings in which Φ\Phi is an RKHS ball.

To achieve Φ\Phi-regret minimization from ℋΦ\mathcal{H}_{\Phi}-multicalibration, a decision maker forecasts the next loss (out of the set ℒ\mathcal{L} of losses that could be incurred), and best responds to it. We provide a formal description in Algorithm 2 and prove its correctness in the following theorem which constitutes our second main result.

Theorem 5.

Let 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} be the sequence of forecast distributions produced in Algorithm 2, and let μt\mu_{t} be the induced distribution over actions zt=σ⁡(pt)z_{t}=\sigma(p_{t}) where pt∼𝒟tp_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}. Then, the Φ\Phi-regret of the resulting decision-making algorithm is upper bounded by the ℋΦ\mathcal{H}_{\Phi}-multicalibration error of the forecaster. For any ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi, if we define hϕ​(p)=σ⁡(p)−ϕ⁡(σ⁡(p))h_{\phi}(p)=\sigma(p)-\phi(\sigma(p)), then:

RegretTΦ​(ϕ)≔∑t=1T𝔼zt∼μt​[ℓt⊤​(zt−ϕ⁡(zt))]≤∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(pt)⊤​(ℓt−pt)]=MC-ErrT​(hϕ).\textrm{Regret}^{\Phi}_{T}(\phi)\coloneqq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{z_{t}\sim\mu_{t}}\Big[\ell_{t}^{\top}(z_{t}-\phi(z_{t}))\Big]\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h(p_{t})^{\top}(\ell_{t}-p_{t})\Big]=\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h_{\phi}).

In particular, sublinear multicalibration error with respect to ℋΦ\mathcal{H}_{\Phi} by the forecaster, guarantees sublinear Φ\Phi-regret by the decision-maker, RegretTΦ≤MC-ErrT\textrm{Regret}^{\Phi}_{T}\leq\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}.

Proof.

For any ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi, by definition of μt\mu_{t} as the pushforward of 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} under p↦σ⁡(p)p\mapsto\sigma(p),

∑t=1T𝔼zt∼μt​[ℓt⊤​(zt−ϕ⁡(zt))]\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{z_{t}\sim\mu_{t}}\Big[\ell_{t}^{\top}(z_{t}-\phi(z_{t}))\Big] =∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[ℓt⊤​(σ⁡(pt)−ϕ⁡(σ⁡(pt)))]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[\ell_{t}^{\top}\big(\sigma(p_{t})-\phi(\sigma(p_{t}))\big)\Big]
=∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[hϕ​(pt)⊤​(ℓt−pt)]+∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[hϕ​(pt)⊤​pt]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h_{\phi}(p_{t})^{\top}(\ell_{t}-p_{t})\Big]+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h_{\phi}(p_{t})^{\top}p_{t}\Big]
≤∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[hϕ​(pt)⊤​(ℓt−pt)],\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h_{\phi}(p_{t})^{\top}(\ell_{t}-p_{t})\Big],

where in the last inequality we used the fact that for every ptp_{t},

hϕ​(pt)⊤​pt=pt⊤​(σ⁡(pt)−ϕ⁡(σ⁡(pt)))≤0h_{\phi}(p_{t})^{\top}p_{t}=p_{t}^{\top}\Big(\sigma(p_{t})-\phi(\sigma(p_{t}))\Big)\leq 0

since σ⁡(pt)\sigma(p_{t}) is the minimizer of pt⊤​zp_{t}^{\top}z over zz in 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. ∎

We note that this entire construction also goes through if we add contexts xtx_{t} into the picture, yielding an efficient reduction from online multicalibration to contextual Φ\Phi-regret. In the contextual version, Nature reveals contexts (features) xt∈𝒳x_{t}\in\mathcal{X} before the decision-maker chooses their action ztz_{t}, and the goal is to minimize

supϕ∈Φ∑t=1T𝔼zt∼μt​[ℓt⊤​(zt−ϕ⁡(xt,zt))],\displaystyle\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{z_{t}\sim\mu_{t}}\Big[\ell_{t}^{\top}(z_{t}-\phi(x_{t},z_{t}))\Big],

where Φ\Phi is now a set of deviations ϕ:𝒳×𝒵→𝒵\phi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{Z}. In this setting, it suffices for the forecaster to be multicalibrated with respect to the functions hϕ​(xt,pt)=σ⁡(pt)−ϕ⁡(xt,σ⁡(pt))h_{\phi}(x_{t},p_{t})=\sigma(p_{t})-\phi(x_{t},\sigma(p_{t})).

As discussed in Section 4, the simplicity of the reduction, together with the previous result (Theorem 4), yields a new path from external to Φ\Phi-regret via EVIs and multicalibration. This construction, builds and generalizes on the work of [53] who illustrated a similar connection between forecasting and decision making for the restricted case where the action set 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is a finite set of actions and the set Φ\Phi contains all endomorphisms. Our work broadens this connection between forecasting and decision making for general sets of actions 𝒵\mathcal{Z} and deviations Φ\Phi.

3 Algorithmic Implications for Online Multicalibration
and Omniprediction

In this section, we examine some of the consequences of our reduction from regret minimization to online multicalibration (Theorem 4). We highlight four main implications.

  1. (a)

    We show that several existing online high-dimensional multicalibration algorithms are special cases of our reduction, thereby unifying their previously disparate analyses. These reinterpretations sometimes yield improved runtimes as well.

  2. (b)

    We demonstrate how the reduction facilitates the technical transfer of ideas between well-studied variants of online learning and online multicalibration, yielding the first known online multicalibration algorithms that succeed in more challenging environments where outcomes are only partially observed.

  3. (c)

    We show how the reduction yields an oracle-efficient algorithm for online omniprediction in the multiclass setting, solving another open problem from [30].

  4. (d)

    We show how our reduction can be used to guarantee calibration with respect to more stringent ℓ1\ell_{1} or ECE notions of multicalibration at optimal rates.

3.1 Unified Analyses and Faster Runtimes for Established Algorithms

Defensive Forecasting is Follow The Regularized Leader over the RKHS Ball.

Defensive Forecasting is an influential, game-theoretic approach to sequential prediction introduced by [62]. Even though it predates the work on multicalibration by [43], it achieves exactly the same guarantee for classes ℋ\mathcal{H} that constitute a reproducing kernel Hilbert space or RKHS. Vovk refers to online multicalibration as resolution [63]. We point the reader to [59] for an overview of work in this area.

As background, a vector-valued RKHS is a Hilbert space of functions ℋ⊆{𝒳×𝒴→ℝd}\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\} defined in terms of a matrix-valued kernel Γ⁡((⋅,⋅),(⋅,⋅))\Gamma((\cdot,\cdot),(\cdot,\cdot)), where Γ⁡((x,p),(x′,p′))∈ℝd×d\Gamma((x,p),(x^{\prime},p^{\prime}))\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. Since it is a Hilbert space, ℋ\mathcal{H} is equipped with an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ℋ\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} and functions satisfy the reproducing property. For every h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} and θ∈ℝd\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, h​(x,p)⊤​θ=⟨Γ⁡(⋅,(x,p))​θ,h⟩ℋh(x,p)^{\top}\theta=\langle\Gamma(\cdot,(x,p))\theta,h\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}.

Here, Γ⁡(⋅,(x,p))\Gamma(\cdot,(x,p)) is the evaluation functional. If Ψ⁡(x,p)∈ℝr×d\Psi(x,p)\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d} is a fixed feature map, then Γ⁡((x,p),(x′,p′))=Ψ​(x,p)⊤​Ψ​(x′,p′)\Gamma((x,p),(x^{\prime},p^{\prime}))=\Psi(x,p)^{\top}\Psi(x^{\prime},p^{\prime}) is a matrix-valued kernel. The RKHS ℋ\mathcal{H} in this case is equal to the closure of the set {(x,p)→Ψ​(x,p)⊤​θ:θ∈ℝr}\{(x,p)\to\Psi(x,p)^{\top}\theta:\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{r}\}.

[20] prove that the defensive forecasting procedure in Algorithm 3, which generalizes the original K29 algorithms from [62, 63] to work efficiently for high-dimensional outcomes, satisfies the following multicalibration guarantee.

Proposition 1 ([20]).

Let ℋ⊆{𝒳×𝒴→ℝd}\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\} be any vector-valued RKHS with matrix-valued kernel Γ⁡((x,p),(x′,p′))\Gamma((x,p),(x^{\prime},p^{\prime})). Then, for any function hh in the RKHS ℋ\mathcal{H}, if εt=1/(10​t2)\varepsilon_{t}=1/(10t^{2}), Algorithm 3 produces distributions 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} such that for any sequence of (xt,yt)(x_{t},y_{t}),

|∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t[h(xt,pt)⊤(yt−pt)]|≤∥h∥ℋ∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​(yt−pt)⊤​Γ​((xt,pt),(xt,pt))​(yt−pt)+1,\displaystyle\bigg|\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\bigr[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\bigr]\bigg|\leq\|h\|_{\mathcal{H}}\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}(y_{t}-p_{t})^{\top}\Gamma((x_{t},p_{t}),(x_{t},p_{t}))(y_{t}-p_{t})+1},

where ‖h‖ℋ2=⟨h,h⟩ℋ\|h\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\langle h,h\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. In the case where Γ⁡((x,p),(x′,p′))=Ψ​(x,p)⊤​Ψ​(x′,p′)\Gamma((x,p),(x^{\prime},p^{\prime}))=\Psi(x,p)^{\top}\Psi(x^{\prime},p^{\prime}) for some feature mapping Ψ⁡(x,p)∈ℝr×d\Psi(x,p)\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}, the guarantee above can be rewritten as: For any hθ​(x,p)=Ψ​(x,p)⊤​θh_{\theta}(x,p)=\Psi(x,p)^{\top}\theta,

|∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t[hθ(xt,pt)⊤(yt−pt)]|≤∥θ∥2∑t=1T‖𝔼pt∼𝒟t​Ψ​(xt,pt)​(yt−pt)‖22+1.\displaystyle\bigg|\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\bigr[h_{\theta}(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\bigr]\bigg|\leq\|\theta\|_{2}\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Psi(x_{t},p_{t})(y_{t}-p_{t})\|_{2}^{2}+1}.

At time tt the algorithm runs in time 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(log⁡(t​D),eval⁡(Γ)))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(\log(tD),\mathrm{eval}(\Gamma))) where D=sup(x,p)‖Γ⁡((x,p),(x,p))‖opD=\sup_{(x,p)}\|\Gamma((x,p),(x,p))\|_{\mathrm{op}} and eval⁡(Γ)\mathrm{eval}(\Gamma) is an upper bound on the time it takes to evaluate the kernel function Γ\Gamma.

Here, we show that Defensive Forecasting is just a special instantiation of our general reduction with follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) over the ℓ2\ell_{2} ball as the regret minimizer. We can therefore reprove its correctness using the following textbook result on FTRL and demystify the origin of the operators SS in Algorithm 3.

Lemma 1 (Theorem 5.2 in [42]).

Consider the follow-the-regularized-leader algorithm for online linear optimization over the ball of radius BB where θ1=0\theta_{1}=0 and for all t>1t>1,

θt=arg​minθ:‖θ‖2≤B{η∑i=1t−1−ℓi⊤θ+∥θ∥22}.\displaystyle\theta_{t}=\argmin_{\theta:\|\theta\|_{2}\leq B}\left\{\eta\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}-\ell_{i}^{\top}\theta+\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}\right\}.

Then, there exists a choice of η\eta such that for all tt, the vectors θt\theta_{t} can be written as

θt=αt​∑i=1t−1ℓi,\displaystyle\theta_{t}=\alpha_{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\ell_{i}, (5)

where αt\alpha_{t} is a positive scalar, and for any θ\theta with ℓ2\ell_{2} norm bounded by BB,

∑t=1Tℓt⊤​θ−∑t=1Tℓt⊤​θt≤2​B​∑t=1T‖ℓt‖2.\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}^{\top}\theta-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}^{\top}\theta_{t}\leq 2B\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|\ell_{t}\|^{2}}. (6)

Plugging in the choice θt\theta_{t} from FTRL in Equation 5 into the expression for hth_{t} from Algorithm 4, and using that ℓi=𝔼pi∼𝒟i​[Ψ⁡(xi,pi)​(yi−pi)]\ell_{i}=\underset{p_{i}\sim\mathcal{D}_{i}}{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[\Psi(x_{i},p_{i})(y_{i}-p_{i})\bigr] we get that:

ht(xt,p)=Ψ(xt,p)⊤θt=αt⋅Ψ(xt,p)⊤∑i=1t−1𝔼pi∼𝒟i[Ψ(xi,pi)(yi−pi)]=αtSt(p).h_{t}(x_{t},p)=\Psi(x_{t},p)^{\top}\theta_{t}=\alpha_{t}\cdot\Psi(x_{t},p)^{\top}\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\underset{p_{i}\sim\mathcal{D}_{i}}{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[\Psi(x_{i},p_{i})(y_{i}-p_{i})\bigr]=\alpha_{t}S_{t}(p).

Since αt>0\alpha_{t}>0 is a positive scalar, the operators over which we are solving EVIs in Algorithm 4, ht​(xt,⋅)h_{t}(x_{t},\cdot), and in Algorithm 3, StS_{t}, are the same up to scaling. For every pp, ht​(xt,p)=αt⋅St​(p)h_{t}(x_{t},p)=\alpha_{t}\cdot S_{t}(p). Therefore, if 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} is an EVI solution over the operator ht​(xt,⋅)h_{t}(x_{t},\cdot) with error ε\varepsilon, then 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} is also an EVI solution over StS_{t} but with error ε/αt\varepsilon/\alpha_{t}. Hence, the distributions 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} that both algorithms select at every time step are essentially identical.

It remains to verify that the two algorithms also have matching multicalibration errors with respect to all functions of the form hθ​(x,p)=Ψ​(x,p)⊤​θh_{\theta}(x,p)=\Psi(x,p)^{\top}\theta. Setting εt=1/(10​t2)\varepsilon_{t}=1/(10t^{2}) in Algorithm 4 gives EVIT=∑t=1Tεt≤1\mathrm{EVI}_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\varepsilon_{t}\leq 1. For the regret term, Lemma 1 yields

RegretT≤2​B​∑t=1T‖ℓt‖2\displaystyle\textrm{Regret}_{T}\leq 2B\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|\ell_{t}\|^{2}} =2​B​∑t=1T‖𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[Ψ⁡(xt,pt)​(yt−pt)]‖22\displaystyle=2B\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Big\|\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\bigl[\Psi(x_{t},p_{t})(y_{t}-p_{t})\bigr]\Big\|^{2}_{2}}
≤2​B​∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[(yt−pt)⊤​Γ​((xt,pt),(xt,pt))​(yt−pt)],\displaystyle\leq 2B\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[(y_{t}-p_{t})^{\top}\Gamma((x_{t},p_{t}),(x_{t},p_{t}))(y_{t}-p_{t})\Big]},

where the last equality uses Γ⁡((x,p),(x′,p′))=Ψ​(x,p)⊤​Ψ​(x′,p′)\Gamma((x,p),(x^{\prime},p^{\prime}))=\Psi(x,p)^{\top}\Psi(x^{\prime},p^{\prime}) and Jensen’s inequality. Applying Theorem 4, the multicalibration error of the distributions produced by Algorithm 4 with respect to any hθ​(x,p)=Ψ​(x,p)⊤​θh_{\theta}(x,p)=\Psi(x,p)^{\top}\theta with ‖θ‖2≤B\|\theta\|_{2}\leq B satisfies

MC-ErrT​(hθ)≤RegretT+EVIT≤2​B​∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[(yt−pt)⊤​Γ​((xt,pt),(xt,pt))​(yt−pt)]+1,\displaystyle\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h_{\theta})\leq\textrm{Regret}_{T}+\mathrm{EVI}_{T}\leq 2B\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[(y_{t}-p_{t})^{\top}\Gamma((x_{t},p_{t}),(x_{t},p_{t}))(y_{t}-p_{t})\Big]}+1,

matching the Defensive Forecasting guarantee of [20] up to a small constant.

Cubically Faster Runtimes for the Unbiased Prediction Algorithm

[53] introduced the first algorithm for online high-dimensional multicalibration. It guarantees multicalibration with respect to any function in the convex hull of a finite collection of functions ℋ\mathcal{H}. We present pseudocode for the unbiased prediction algorithm in Algorithm 5.

Here, we provide a simplified proof of its correctness via Theorem 4 and improve its runtime from Ω⁡(T3)\Omega(T^{3}) to O~​(T)\widetilde{O}(T). In particular, the procedure exactly matches the template of our reduction with a specific choice of regret minimizer and EVI solver (it is, in effect, an improved version of the Hedge procedure we presented in Section 2). We can reprove its correctness by simply plugging in the regret bound from [10] into Theorem 4.

Corollary 1.

The Unbiased Prediction Algorithm produces distributions such that for any h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H},

∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​h​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)≤𝒪~​(log⁡(|ℋ|)⋅∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]2).\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\leq\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\sqrt{\log(|\mathcal{H}|)\cdot\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\Big]^{2}}\right).
Proof.

[10] prove that for any sequence of losses ℓt\ell_{t}, the Multiscale Multiplicative Weights with Correction algorithm produces hth_{t} such that for any h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H},

RegretT​(h)=∑t=1Tft​(ht)−∑t=1Tft​(h)≤𝒪~​(log⁡(|ℋ|)​∑t=1Tft​(h)2).\displaystyle\textrm{Regret}_{T}(h)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(h_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(h)\leq\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\sqrt{\log(|\mathcal{H}|)\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(h)^{2}}\right). (7)

By Theorem 4, the multicalibration error is bounded by RegretT​(h)+EVIT\textrm{Regret}_{T}(h)+\mathrm{EVI}_{T}. Since [53] set εt≤1/t\varepsilon_{t}\leq 1/t, then EVIT=∑t=1Tεt=∑t=1Tt−1≤𝒪⁡(log⁡(T))\mathrm{EVI}_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\varepsilon_{t}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}t^{-1}\leq\mathcal{O}(\log(T)). The stated regret bound follows from substituting in the fact that ft​(h)=−𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]f_{t}(h)=-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\Big]. ∎

As a comment, here we present the regret bound from [53] in a slightly different form, where we let ℋ⊆{𝒳×𝒴→ℝd}\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\} be any finite set of functions. To recover the exact bound in [53], we can pick {(x,p)→s⋅ei→⋅c(x,p):c∈𝒞,i∈[d],s∈{±1}}\{(x,p)\to s\cdot\vec{e_{i}}\cdot c(x,p):c\in\mathcal{C},i\in[d],s\in\{\pm 1\}\} where 𝒞⊆{𝒳×𝒴→{0,1}}\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\{0,1\}\} is a finite set of binary functions and e→i\vec{e}_{i} denotes the iith standard basis vector in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Recall that to solve EVIs via regret minimization algorithms, we need to run the regret minimizer for kk such rounds where kk satisfies Regret​(k)/k≤εt\textrm{Regret}(k)/k\leq\varepsilon_{t}. Setting εt=1/t\varepsilon_{t}=1/t as in [53], since Regret​(k)\textrm{Regret}(k) is Θ⁡(k)\Theta(\sqrt{k}), we need to set k≥Ω⁡(t2)k\geq\Omega(t^{2}). The total runtime of the algorithm is then lower bounded by ∑t=1TΩ⁡(t2)≥Ω⁡(T3)\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Omega(t^{2})\geq\Omega(T^{3}). However, by swapping out the EVI solver for the ellipsoid-based procedure from [65], we can improve the runtime to 𝒪⁡(T​log⁡T)\mathcal{O}(T\log T). We summarize this statement formally below.

Proposition 2.

Fix a finite class of functions ℋ⊆{𝒳×𝒴→ℝd}\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\} and consider the version of the unbiased prediction algorithm where the EVI solving procedure in line 4 is replaced with the ellipsoid algorithm from [65] which solves EVIs to precision ε\varepsilon in time log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon). Then this modified procedure achieves an identical MC-ErrT\textrm{MC-Err}_{T} for every h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} to that presented in Corollary 1, yet the runtime over TT rounds is 𝒪~​(T⋅poly​(|ℋ|))\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T\cdot\mathrm{poly}(|\mathcal{H}|)) instead of Ω⁡(T3⋅poly⁡(|ℋ|))\Omega(T^{3}\cdot\mathrm{poly}(|\mathcal{H}|)) as in Algorithm 5.

3.2 New Online Multicalibration Algorithms for Complex Environments

We move on to the second set of implications of Theorem 4, showing how it directly enables online multicalibration algorithms with provable guarantees in richer environments.

3.2.1 Online Multicalibration with Delayed Observations

One immediate implication of Theorem 4 is that it allows us to design algorithms which guarantee online multicalibration even when outcomes yty_{t} are not immediately observed.

To motivate the problem, consider the setting where at every day tt, a doctor predicts the likelihood of a patient having a particular disease, yet the presence or absence of this disease is not revealed until the patient comes for a follow-up visit at some future date t′=t+dtt^{\prime}=t+d_{t} where dtd_{t} is a positive integer delay. Even though the outcome is not observed for another dtd_{t} days, the doctor still needs to make predictions for all patients who arrive between tt and t′t^{\prime}. Furthermore, different patients might have different visit schedules, hence the delays dtd_{t} are unknown and can vary with tt.

Despite these difficulties, the doctor aims to make predictions that are not just calibrated, but multicalibrated without making any assumptions about how the data is generated. That is, they aim to sequentially produce predictions that satisfy the following definition:

Definition 4 (Online Multicalibration under Delayed Observations).

Fix ℋ⊆{𝒳×𝒴→ℝd}\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\} and consider the following online protocol where at every time tt, Nature selects features xtx_{t} and reveals previous outcomes {yi:i+di=t,di>0}\{y_{i}:i+d_{i}=t,d_{i}>0\} to the Learner. Then, the Learner outputs a distribution 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} over predictions ptp_{t}.

An algorithm guarantees online multicalibration under delays with respect to ℋ\mathcal{H} if it selects 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} such that regardless of the feature, outcome pairs (xt,yt)(x_{t},y_{t}) and delays dtd_{t} chosen by Nature, for any h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H},

MC-ErrT​(h)=∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]=o⁡(T).\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\Big]=o(T).

Note that this setup generalizes the standard online setting studied so far where the Learner immediately sees the outcomes yty_{t} after selecting 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}. In this case, dt=1d_{t}=1 for all tt. To the best of our knowledge, our work initiates the study of this problem. Using our reduction, we can design simple algorithms that achieve this guarantee by leveraging the fact that there are by now many online learning algorithms that can handle delayed losses as per the following definition.

Definition 5.

Fix a set ℋ\mathcal{H} and consider the protocol where at every round tt, Nature reveals a set of prior losses {ℓi:i+di=t}\{\ell_{i}:i+d_{i}=t\} to the Learner, who then selects hth_{t}. An algorithm guarantees no-regret in this online learning with delays protocol if

RegretT​(h)≔∑t=1Tℓt​(ht)−∑t=1Tℓt​(h)=o⁡(T)\textrm{Regret}_{T}(h)\coloneqq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}(h_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}(h)=o(T)

for all h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H}.

We show that our main reduction between regret minimization and online multicalibration handles this extension seamlessly. The key insight is that Algorithm 1 has two main parts: the EVI solver and the online Learner that produces hth_{t}. Even though losses are not observed until a later time step, the online Learner in Definition 5 still produces a solution hth_{t} at every time tt, and this is enough to produce the distribution 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} since the EVI solver only needs hth_{t}.

Corollary 2.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be any algorithm that guarantees RegretT\textrm{Regret}_{T} in the online learning with delays protocol with respect to ℋ\mathcal{H} as per Definition 5. Then, using 𝒜\mathcal{A} as the external regret minimizer in Algorithm 1 guarantees online multicalibration with delays as per Definition 4. For any h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H},

MC-ErrT​(h)≤RegretT​(h)+EVIT.\displaystyle\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h)\leq\textrm{Regret}_{T}(h)+\textrm{EVI}_{T}.

As a specific example consider the case where hθ​(xt,pt)=Ψ​(xt,pt)⊤​θh_{\theta}(x_{t},p_{t})=\Psi(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}\theta (for simplicity, we will use hθh_{\theta} and θ\theta interchangeably in this derivation) for some fixed feature map Ψ⁡(x,p)∈ℝr×d\Psi(x,p)\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}. [60] proved that there exists a choice of constant step size η\eta such that the following online gradient descent procedure, where we update the parameters asynchronously on the basis of the losses observed at time tt, ℒt={ℓs:s+ds=t}\mathcal{L}_{t}=\{\ell_{s}:s+d_{s}=t\},

θt+1=Π𝔹2​[θt−η​∑ℓs∈ℒt∇ℓs​(θs)],\displaystyle\theta_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathbb{B}_{2}}\left[\theta_{t}-\eta\sum_{\ell_{s}\in\mathcal{L}_{t}}\nabla\ell_{s}(\theta_{s})\right],

satisfies the following regret bound for any θ\theta with ℓ2\ell_{2} norm at most 1:

∑t=1Tℓt​(θt)−∑t=1Tℓt​(θ)≤𝒪⁡(max1≤t≤T⁡‖∇ℓt​(θt)‖2​T+∑t=1Tdt).\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}(\theta_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}(\theta)\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\max_{1\leq t\leq T}\|\nabla\ell_{t}(\theta_{t})\|_{2}\sqrt{T+\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t}}\right).

Setting εt=1/t\varepsilon_{t}=1/\sqrt{t} and bounding EVIT≤𝒪⁡(T)\textrm{EVI}_{T}\leq\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}), this implies the following end-to-end bound for online multicalibration with delays for any hθ=Ψ​(x,p)⊤​θh_{\theta}=\Psi(x,p)^{\top}\theta where θ\theta is in the unit ball:

MC-ErrT​(hθ)≤𝒪⁡(max1≤t≤T⁡‖𝔼pt∼𝒟t​Ψ​(xt,pt)​(yt−pt)‖2​T+∑t=1Tdt).\displaystyle\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h_{\theta})\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\max_{1\leq t\leq T}\|\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Psi(x_{t},p_{t})(y_{t}-p_{t})\|_{2}\sqrt{T+\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t}}\right).

The bound is o⁡(T)o(T) as long as ∑t=1Tdt\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t} is o⁡(T2)o(T^{2}).

3.2.2 Online Multicalibration under Censored Outcomes

In many real-world decision-making settings, the true outcome yty_{t} is censored: we observe yty_{t} only if the predictions ptp_{t} fall within a specific range. For example, in lending, we only observe whether people repay loans if we issue them loans, a decision that occurs only if the predicted likelihood of repayment ptp_{t} is not too small.

Here, we slightly modify our reduction to design the first known algorithms for online multicalibration under censoring. The main modification we need is to add importance sampling into our reduction, as in prior work on online learning (e.g., [9]). We start by formally defining the online multicalibration with censored observations problem:

Definition 6 (Online Multicalibration under Censored Observations).

Fix a class of functions ℋ⊆{𝒳×𝒴→ℝd}\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\} and a censoring function C:Δ⁡(𝒴)→{0,1}C:\Delta(\mathcal{Y})\to\{0,1\}. Consider the online protocol where at every time tt, Nature selects (xt,yt)(x_{t},y_{t}) and then reveals xtx_{t} to the Learner who outputs a distribution 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} over predictions ptp_{t}. Lastly, Nature reveals yty_{t} to the Learner if C⁡(𝒟t)=1C(\mathcal{D}_{t})=1.

An algorithm guarantees online multicalibration under censored observations with respect to ℋ\mathcal{H} if, regardless of Nature’s choices, the following holds for every h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H},

MC-ErrT​(h)=∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]=o⁡(T).\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\left[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\right]=o(T).

We note that in the definition, the multicalibration error is summed over all rounds TT, regardless of whether the Learner observed the outcome yty_{t} in any given round tt. Also, unlike in previous versions, yty_{t} is selected non-adaptively: Nature selects yty_{t} before the Learner chooses the distribution 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}. Without loss of generality (since the Learner knows the censoring function C⁡(⋅)C(\cdot)), we will assume that there is a known 𝒟⋆\mathcal{D}_{\star} such that if 𝒟t=𝒟⋆\mathcal{D}_{t}=\mathcal{D}_{\star}, then C⁡(𝒟⋆)=1C(\mathcal{D}_{\star})=1 and yty_{t} is observed.

Proposition 3.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be any online algorithm that selects hth_{t} such that for any h∈ℋ,γ>0h\in\mathcal{H},\gamma>0, and sequence of losses f^t\hat{f}_{t} that are linear in hh and 1/γ1/\gamma

RegretT,1/γ≔suph∈ℋ∑t=1Tft^​(ht)−∑t=1Tf^t​(h)=o⁡(T).\displaystyle\textrm{Regret}_{T,1/\gamma}\coloneqq\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat{f_{t}}(h_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat{f}_{t}(h)=o(T).

Then, using 𝒜\mathcal{A} as the no-regret learner in Algorithm 6 satisfies the following online multicalibration under censored observations error (Definition 6) with respect to functions in ℋ\mathcal{H},

MC-ErrT≤γ​L​T+EVIT+𝔼Z1,…,ZT​[RegretT,1/γ].\displaystyle\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}\leq\gamma LT+\textrm{EVI}_{T}+\mathbb{E}_{Z_{1},\dots,Z_{T}}[\textrm{Regret}_{T,1/\gamma}].

Here, LL is a uniform upper bound on |h​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)||h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})|.

Proof.

Fix any h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H}. By definition of 𝒟~t\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{t},

∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟~t​[h​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{t}}\left[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\right] =(1−γ)​∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]\displaystyle=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim{\mathcal{D}}_{t}}\left[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\right]
+γ∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟⋆[h(xt,pt)⊤(yt−pt)].\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pt+\gamma\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim{\mathcal{D}_{\star}}}\left[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\right].

By assumption, the second term is bounded by γ​L​T\gamma LT and by the EVI guarantee,

0≤εt−𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[ht​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)].\displaystyle 0\leq\varepsilon_{t}-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}[h_{t}(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})].

Using these two facts, we get that MC-ErrT​(h)\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h) is at most

γ​L​T+∑t=1Tεt+∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(xt,p)⊤​(yt−pt)]−𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[ht​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)].\displaystyle\gamma LT+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\varepsilon_{t}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim{\mathcal{D}}_{t}}\left[h(x_{t},p)^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\right]-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim{\mathcal{D}}_{t}}\left[h_{t}(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\right].

Next, we observe that for any hh, 𝔼Zt​[f^​(h)]=−𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[h​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)]\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}}[\hat{f}(h)]=-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim{\mathcal{D}}_{t}}\left[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\right]. Therefore, using linearity of expectation, we can rewrite the above as

γ​L​T+∑t=1Tεt+∑t=1T𝔼Zt​[f^t​(ht)−f^t​(h)]=γ​L​T+EVIT+𝔼Z1,…,ZT​[RegretT,1/γ].∎\gamma LT+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\varepsilon_{t}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}}[\hat{f}_{t}(h_{t})-\hat{f}_{t}(h)]=\gamma LT+\textrm{EVI}_{T}+\mathbb{E}_{Z_{1},\dots,Z_{T}}[\textrm{Regret}_{T,1/\gamma}].\qed

Since RegretT,1/γ\textrm{Regret}_{T,1/\gamma} typically scales linearly with 1/γ1/\gamma, by tuning γ\gamma, we get a sublinear regret bound. As an example, if we run the Multiplicative Weights algorithm, we get that

RegretT,1/γ≤𝒪~​(log⁡(|ℋ|)​T​L2/γ2).\displaystyle\textrm{Regret}_{T,1/\gamma}\leq\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\sqrt{\log(|\mathcal{H}|)TL^{2}/\gamma^{2}}\right).

Optimizing over γ\gamma to balance between terms, we get a 𝒪~​(T3/4)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{3/4}) rate for this problem by running Multiplicative Weights (Hedge) as the online Learner.

Remark 1 (Dynamic Multicalibration).

This list of consequences is by no means exhaustive. For instance, we could also guarantee dynamic multicalibration regret bounds of the form

∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​ht​(xt,pt)⊤​(yt−pt)=o⁡(T),\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}h_{t}(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})=o(T),

where one can specify the sequence of functions {ht}t=1T\{h_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} (that change over time, yet have bounded path length) by plugging in dynamic, path-dependent regret bounds into our reduction.

3.3 Oracle-Efficient Algorithms for Online, Multiclass Omniprediction

To close this section, we show how by leveraging our reduction together with known connections between multicalibration and omniprediction [33, 32], we can derive simple algorithms for multiclass omniprediction that are efficient whenever online learning is efficient.

We start by defining online omniprediction for multiclass outcomes yy. For ptp_{t} in the simplex, we write y~t∼pt\tilde{y}_{t}\sim p_{t} to denote outcomes y~t\tilde{y}_{t} sampled from the conditional distribution specified by ptp_{t}.44 4 If ptp_{t} is in the simplex, then we can write pt,i=Pr[y~t=i]p_{t,i}=\Pr[\tilde{y}_{t}=i] for every i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k. Furthermore, for multiclass outcomes yy, we adopt the notation y→=(1{y=1},…,1{y=k})\vec{y}=(1\{y=1\},\dots,1\{y=k\}) to denote the one-hot encoded version of yy.

Definition 7.

Consider the protocol in which, at each time step, Nature reveals features xtx_{t}, the Learner chooses a distribution 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} over forecasts pt∈Δk={p∈ℝk:pi≥0,∑i=1kpi=1}p_{t}\in\Delta_{k}=\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{k}:p_{i}\geq 0,\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_{i}=1\}, and Nature reveals the true outcome yt∈[k]={1,…,k}y_{t}\in[k]=\{1,\dots,k\}.

Fix a set of actions 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. Let ℒ⊆{𝒵×[k]→ℝ≥0}\mathcal{L}\subseteq\{\mathcal{Z}\times[k]\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\} be a set of loss functions and 𝒞⊆{𝒳→𝒵}\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Z}\} be a set of decision rules. An online algorithm is an omnipredictor with respect to ℒ\mathcal{L} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} if it produces distributions 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} such that for every ℓ∈ℒ\ell\in\mathcal{L} and πℓ​(pt)=arg​minz∈𝒵⁡𝔼y~t∼pt​ℓ​(z,y~t)\pi_{\ell}(p_{t})=\argmin_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{y}_{t}\sim p_{t}}\ell(z,\tilde{y}_{t}),

∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[ℓ⁡(πℓ​(pt),yt)]≤min⁡∑t=1Tc∈𝒞⁡ℓ⁡(c⁡(xt),yt)+o⁡(T).\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\left[\ell(\pi_{\ell}(p_{t}),y_{t})\right]\leq\min_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell(c(x_{t}),y_{t})+o(T).

Intuitively, an omnipredictor is an algorithm that produces predictions that can be postprocessed to yield good decisions. They guarantee that the best response function to any function ℓ\ell,

πℓ(pt)=arg​minz∈𝒵𝔼y~t∼ptℓ(z,y~t)=arg​minz∈𝒵∑i=1kℓ(z,i)⋅pt,i,\displaystyle\pi_{\ell}(p_{t})=\argmin_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{y}_{t}\sim p_{t}}\ell(z,\tilde{y}_{t})=\argmin_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\ell(z,i)\cdot p_{t,i},

has low excess risk to the best decision rule in 𝒞\mathcal{C} for that loss ℓ\ell. Note that by definition, the postprocessing of ptp_{t} has lower loss than any decision rule c:𝒳→𝒵c:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z} on outcomes sampled from ptp_{t}:

𝔼y~∼p​[ℓ⁡(πℓ​(pt),y~)]≤𝔼y~∼p​[ℓ⁡(h⁡(x),y~)].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{y}\sim p}[\ell(\pi_{\ell}(p_{t}),\tilde{y})]\leq\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{y}\sim p}[\ell(h(x),\tilde{y})].

It is by now well known [33, 30, 32, 16, 49] that given any set of loss functions ℒ\mathcal{L} and decision rules 𝒞\mathcal{C}, one can construct a set of test functions ℋℒ,𝒞\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}} (defined in terms of ℒ\mathcal{L} and 𝒞\mathcal{C}) such that multicalibration with respect to ℋℒ,𝒞\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}} implies online omniprediction with respect to ℒ\mathcal{L} and 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

What is new in our work is that by exploiting this connection, and our new path between regret minimization and online multicalibration, we establish a path between regret minimization and omniprediction that yields oracle-efficient algorithms for omniprediction.

We start by stating the following (now folklore) lemma, which we specialize to the multiclass setting, proving that multicalibration implies omniprediction.

Lemma 2.

Fix a class of loss functions ℒ⊆{𝒵×[k]→ℝ≥0}\mathcal{L}\subseteq\{\mathcal{Z}\times[k]\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\} and a set of decision rules 𝒞⊆{𝒳→𝒵}\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Z}\}. Define the set of test functions

ℋℒ,𝒞={hℓ:ℓ∈ℒ}∪{hℓ,c:ℓ∈ℒ,c∈𝒞}⊆{𝒳×Δk→ℝd}\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}}=\{h_{\ell}:\ell\in\mathcal{L}\}\cup\{h_{\ell,c}:\ell\in\mathcal{L},c\in\mathcal{C}\}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\times\Delta_{k}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\} (8)

where hℓh_{\ell} and hℓ,ch_{\ell,c} are defined as:

hℓ​(pt)\displaystyle h_{\ell}(p_{t}) ≔(ℓ⁡(πℓ​(pt),1),…,ℓ⁡(πℓ​(pt),k))⊤∈ℝk\displaystyle\coloneqq\big(\ell(\pi_{\ell}(p_{t}),1),\dots,\ell(\pi_{\ell}(p_{t}),k)\big)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}
hℓ,c​(xt)\displaystyle h_{\ell,c}(x_{t}) ≔−(ℓ⁡(c⁡(xt),1),…,ℓ⁡(c⁡(xt),k))⊤∈ℝk.\displaystyle\coloneqq-\big(\ell(c(x_{t}),1),\dots,\ell(c(x_{t}),k)\big)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}.

If an online algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} produces distributions 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} with multicalibration error bounded by MC-ErrT\textrm{MC-Err}_{T} with respect to ℋℒ,𝒞\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}}, then 𝒜\mathcal{A} is an omnipredictor with respect to ℒ\mathcal{L} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} with omniprediction error bounded by 2​MC-ErrT2\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}. That is, for every ℓ∈ℒ\ell\in\mathcal{L},

∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[ℓ⁡(πℓ​(pt),yt)]≤min⁡∑t=1Tc∈𝒞⁡ℓ⁡(c⁡(xt),yt)+2​MC-ErrT.\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\left[\ell(\pi_{\ell}(p_{t}),y_{t})\right]\leq\min_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell(c(x_{t}),y_{t})+2\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}.
Proof.

The proof follows the same template pioneered by [32], showing that outcome indistinguishability implies omniprediction. In particular, using the notation y~t∼pt\tilde{y}_{t}\sim p_{t} to denote sampling a multiclass outcome from the distribution specified by pt∈Δkp_{t}\in\Delta_{k} where Pr[y~=i]=pt,i\Pr[\tilde{y}=i]=p_{t,i}, we have the following rewriting,
