∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[ℓ⁡(πℓ​(pt),yt)]−∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟ty~t∼pt​[ℓ⁡(πℓ​(pt),y~t)]\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\underset{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}{\mathbb{E}}[\ell(\pi_{\ell}(p_{t}),y_{t})]-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\underset{\tilde{y}_{t}\sim p_{t}}{\underset{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}{\mathbb{E}}}[\ell(\pi_{\ell}(p_{t}),\tilde{y}_{t})] =∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[hℓ​(pt)⊤​(y→t−pt)]≤MC-ErrT\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\left[h_{\ell}(p_{t})^{\top}(\vec{y}_{t}-p_{t})\right]\leq\textrm{MC-Err}_{T} (9)
∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟ty~t∼pt​[ℓ⁡(c⁡(xt),y~t)]−∑t=1Tℓ⁡(c⁡(xt),yt)\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\underset{\tilde{y}_{t}\sim p_{t}}{\underset{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}{\mathbb{E}}}[\ell(c(x_{t}),\tilde{y}_{t})]-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell(c(x_{t}),y_{t}) =∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[hℓ,c​(xt)⊤​(y→t−pt)]≤MC-ErrT.\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\left[h_{\ell,c}(x_{t})^{\top}(\vec{y}_{t}-p_{t})\right]\leq\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}. (10)

Using these inequalities, for any function ℓ∈ℒ\ell\in\mathcal{L} and c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}, we have that,

∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[ℓ⁡(πℓ​(pt),yt)]\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}[\ell(\pi_{\ell}(p_{t}),y_{t})] ≤∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟ty~t∼pt​[ℓ⁡(πℓ​(pt),y~)]+MC-ErrT\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\underset{\tilde{y}_{t}\sim p_{t}}{\underset{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}{\mathbb{E}}}\bigl[\ell(\pi_{\ell}(p_{t}),\tilde{y})\bigr]+\textrm{MC-Err}_{T} (By Equation 9)
≤∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟ty~t∼pt​[ℓ⁡(c⁡(xt),y~t)]+MC-ErrT\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\underset{\tilde{y}_{t}\sim p_{t}}{\underset{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}{\mathbb{E}}}[\ell(c(x_{t}),\tilde{y}_{t})]+\textrm{MC-Err}_{T} (By definition of π⁡(pt)\pi(p_{t}))
≤∑t=1Tℓ⁡(c⁡(xt),yt)+2​MC-ErrT.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell(c(x_{t}),y_{t})+2\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}\,. (By Equation 10)

Since ℓ\ell and cc were arbitrary, the argument holds for the best c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}, thereby proving the lemma. ∎

Using this lemma, and our black-box reduction between multicalibration and online learning Theorem 4, we get the following oracle-efficient algorithm for omniprediction.

Corollary 3.

Fix a class of loss functions ℒ\mathcal{L} and decision rules 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Define the class of test functions ℋℒ,𝒞\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}} as in Equation 8 and let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an online algorithm that guarantees external regret at most RegretT\textrm{Regret}_{T} with respect to ℋℒ,𝒞\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}}, as per Equation 2. Then, if the EVI errors are εt\varepsilon_{t}, using 𝒜\mathcal{A} in Algorithm 1 yields omniprediction error bounded by 2​RegretT+∑tεt2\textrm{Regret}_{T}+\sum_{t}\varepsilon_{t}.

In short, this corollary is an end-to-end reduction between omniprediction and online learning. Depending on the pair (ℒ,𝒞)(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}), there are many online algorithms one could use to guarantee omniprediction. For instance, one could always run Multiplicative Weights over finite classes (ℒ,𝒞)(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}) and get an online omniprediction algorithm with error bounded by 𝒪⁡(T​log⁡(|ℒ|⋅|𝒞|))\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T\log(|\mathcal{L}|\cdot|\mathcal{C}|)}). If (ℒ,𝒞)(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}) belongs to an RKHS, one could run defensive forecasting algorithms (see, e.g., [16, 20]) and get a T\sqrt{T} bound with additional dependence on the norms of the functions in the RKHS.

[55] present oracle efficient algorithms for the specific case of omniprediction with respect to binary outcomes. Relative to their work, our results hold for general multiclass settings. Furthermore, our construction can also be extended to work for general real-valued or vector-valued outcomes by using ideas in [49, 34] where one rewrites nonlinear loss functions as linear functions of a high-dimensional vector of statistics. We omit this construction to keep our presentation short.

3.4 Optimal Rates for (Swap) ECE Multicalibration

A large fraction of the calibration literature has focused on achieving what is known as low expected (multi)calibration error, which we refer to as ℓ1\ell_{1} (or ECE) multicalibration. Relative to our notion, where we define a general class of functions ℋ⊆{𝒳×𝒴→ℝd}\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}\} and guarantee that

suph∈ℋ∑t=1T𝔼p∼𝒟t​[h​(xt,p)⊤​(yt−p)]\displaystyle\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}[h(x_{t},p)^{\top}(y_{t}-p)]

is small, in this alternative definition, we fix a class of groups 𝒞⊆𝒳→0,1\mathcal{C}\subseteq{\mathcal{X}\rightarrow{0,1}} and sum up the calibration errors over bins defined in terms of the realized forecasts ptp_{t}.

To simplify our presentation, we focus on the case where 𝒴=[0,1]d\mathcal{Y}=[0,1]^{d} is the dd-dimensional hypercube; however, similar constructions apply to other compact, convex sets.

We let

V≔{0,1/N,…,1}d⊂𝒴V\coloneqq\{0,1/N,\ldots,1\}^{d}\subset\mathcal{Y}

be a grid of size (N+1)d(N+1)^{d} and let {Bv}v∈V\{B_{v}\}_{v\in V} be the partition of [0,1]d[0,1]^{d} into axis-aligned hypercubes of side length 1/N1/N centered at each v∈Vv\in V. Given this notation, we define swap ECE multicalibration:

Definition 8 (Swap ECE Multicalibration).

Consider the online protocol where at every time tt, Nature selects features xt∈𝒳x_{t}\in\mathcal{X}, and then the Learner produces a distribution 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} over forecasts pt∈𝒴=[0,1]dp_{t}\in\mathcal{Y}=[0,1]^{d}. Lastly, Nature reveals the outcome yt∈𝒴y_{t}\in\mathcal{Y}.

We say that an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} guarantees swap ECE multicalibration with respect to 𝒞⊆{𝒳→{0,1}}\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{0,1\}\} and VV, if for any δ>0\delta>0,

SwapECET(𝒞)=∑i=1d∑v∈Vsupc∈𝒞|∑t=1Tc(xt) 1{pt∈Bv}(yt,i−vi)|\displaystyle\mathrm{SwapECE}_{T}(\mathcal{C})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{v\in V}\sup_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\biggl|\sum_{t=1}^{T}c(x_{t})\,1\{p_{t}\in B_{v}\}\,(y_{t,i}-v_{i})\biggr|

is o⁡(T)o(T) with probability 1−δ1-\delta regardless of Nature’s choices of (xt,yt)(x_{t},y_{t}). Here, ptp_{t} is drawn from 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}. Nature chooses yty_{t} with knowledge of 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}, but not of ptp_{t}.

In this section, we show that by using a specific choice of no-regret algorithm within our main reduction (Algorithm 1), we can also achieve this notion of multicalibration as well. In doing so, we highlight how our generalized definition allows for simpler analyses for a wide range of problems that lie downstream of multicalibration (e.g. omniprediction).

The construction is very simple. Given any finite set 𝒞\mathcal{C}, define the finite class of test functions

ℋ𝒞={(x,p)↦s⋅c(x)⋅1{p∈Bv}⋅ei:c∈𝒞,v∈V,s∈{±1},i∈[d]},\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{C}}\;=\;\bigl\{(x,p)\mapsto s\cdot c(x)\cdot 1\{p\in B_{v}\}\cdot e_{i}\;:\;c\in\mathcal{C},\;v\in V,\;s\in\{\pm 1\},\;i\in[d]\bigr\}, (11)

where eie_{i} is the ii-th standard basis vector, so that h(x,p)⊤(y−p)=s⋅c(x)⋅1{p∈Bv}(yi−pi)h(x,p)^{\top}(y-p)=s\cdot c(x)\cdot 1\{p\in B_{v}\}(y_{i}-p_{i}) is a scalar. We have |ℋ𝒞|=2​|𝒞|​(N+1)d​d|\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{C}}|=2|\mathcal{C}|(N+1)^{d}d.

Applying Algorithm 1 with the Multiscale Multiplicative Weights with Correction algorithm [10] as the external regret minimizer over ℋ𝒞\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{C}}, and solving each EVI to precision εt=1/t2\varepsilon_{t}=1/t^{2} so that EVIT≤𝒪⁡(1)\textrm{EVI}_{T}\leq\mathcal{O}(1), we obtain from Theorem 4 that for every h∈ℋ𝒞h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{C}},

MC-ErrT​(h)≤RegretT​(h)+𝒪⁡(1).\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h)\;\leq\;\textrm{Regret}_{T}(h)+\mathcal{O}(1).

Recall from Corollary 1 (Equation 7) that this no-regret algorithm guarantees that

RegretT​(h)=∑t=1Tft​(ht)−∑t=1Tft​(h)≤𝒪~​(log⁡(|ℋ𝒞|)​∑t=1Tft​(h)2).\displaystyle\textrm{Regret}_{T}(h)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(h_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(h)\leq\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\sqrt{\log(|\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{C}}|)\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(h)^{2}}\right).

By definition of the losses in Algorithm 1, taking a generic test function hh from ℋ𝒞\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{C}} (11) indexed by (c,v,s,i)(c,v,s,i) we have that

ft(h)=−𝔼pt∼𝒟t[h(xt,pt)⊤(yt−pt)]=−s𝔼pt∼𝒟t[c(xt)1{pt∈Bv}(yt,i−pt,i)].f_{t}(h)\;=\;-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\bigl[h(x_{t},p_{t})^{\top}(y_{t}-p_{t})\bigr]=-s\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\bigl[c(x_{t})1\{p_{t}\in B_{v}\}(y_{t,i}-p_{t,i})\bigr].

Furthermore, since 1{p∈Bv}2=1{p∈Bv}1\{p\in B_{v}\}^{2}=1\{p\in B_{v}\} and (yt,i−pt,i)2≤1(y_{t,i}-p_{t,i})^{2}\leq 1, Jensen’s inequality gives

ft(h)2≤𝔼pt∼𝒟t[1{pt∈Bv}]=Prpt∼𝒟t[pt∈Bv]≕qv,t.\displaystyle f_{t}(h)^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}[1\{p_{t}\in B_{v}\}]=\Pr_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}[p_{t}\in B_{v}]\eqqcolon q_{v,t}.

Putting all of this together, we get that,

MC-ErrT​(h)≤𝒪~​(log⁡|ℋ𝒞|⋅∑t=1Tqv,t)=𝒪~​(log⁡|ℋ𝒞|⋅Nv),\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h)\;\leq\;\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(\sqrt{\log|\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{C}}|\cdot\sum_{t=1}^{T}q_{v,t}}\right)\;=\;\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(\sqrt{\log|\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{C}}|\cdot N_{v}}\right),

where Nv≔∑tqv,tN_{v}\coloneqq\sum_{t}q_{v,t} is the expected number of rounds in which the forecast lands in bin BvB_{v}. Since for every h∈ℋ𝒞h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{C}}, the function −h-h is also in ℋ𝒞\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{C}}, we can take absolute values and conclude that for every c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}, and v∈Vv\in V: i∈[d]i\in[d]:

|∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t[c(xt) 1{pt∈Bv}(yt,i−pt,i)]|≤𝒪~(log⁡|ℋ𝒞|⋅Nv).\displaystyle\biggl|\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\bigl[c(x_{t})\,1\{p_{t}\in B_{v}\}\,(y_{t,i}-p_{t,i})\bigr]\biggr|\leq\ \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(\sqrt{\log|\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{C}}|\cdot N_{v}}\right). (12)

≤𝔼[c(xt)2 1{pt∈Bv}2(yt,i−pt,i)2∣ℱt−1]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[c(x_{t})^{2}\,1\{p_{t}\in B_{v}\}^{2}\,(y_{t,i}-p_{t,i})^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\right]

≤𝒪~​(d​(N+1)d⋅T⋅d​log⁡(d⋅|𝒞|⋅N))+d​T2​N.\displaystyle\leq\;\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(d\sqrt{(N+1)^{d}\cdot T\cdot d\log(d\cdot|\mathcal{C}|\cdot N)}\right)+\frac{dT}{2N}.

Corollary 4.

Let 𝒞⊆{𝒳→{0,1}}\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\}\} be a finite class. The forecaster produced by Algorithm 1 with the Multiscale Multiplicative Weights with Correction algorithm [10] as the regret minimizer over ℋ𝒞\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{C}} defined as in Equation 11 with N≍(T/d)1/(d+2)N\asymp(T/d)^{1/(d+2)} guarantees that with probability 1−δ1-\delta

In 1 dimension, the bound becomes 𝒪~​(T2/3)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3}) which is the optimal rate for this problem as recently shown by [12]. The T(d+1)/(d+2)T^{(d+1)/(d+2)} rate is in fact optimal for general d>1d>1 [11].

Remark 2.

We highlight how this stands in contrast to the definition of multicalibration (Definition 1) we study for which T\sqrt{T} rates are achievable even in the high-dimensional setting. We hope that this ECE result illustrates to the reader why we focus on the version of multicalibration from Definition 1. While it can be used, as per Corollary 4, to guarantee more stringent notions of calibration such as this ECE result, it is already strong enough to imply other desiderata like omniprediction (see e.g. the previous subsection) and Φ\Phi-regret minimization with sharp T\sqrt{T} rates, rates that are not achievable via arguments that depend on ECE versions of calibration.

Lastly, we remark that this construction provides a unifying analysis of previous algorithms for ECE calibration of a scalar outcome (𝒴=[0,1]\mathcal{Y}=[0,1]) such as [44]. While these run separate instantiations of online algorithms per bin, our simplified construction built on EVIs uses a single online learning routine.

4 Algorithmic Implications for Φ\Phi-Regret Minimization

We now expand on how our new path between external regret minimization and Φ\Phi-regret minimization, via multicalibration and EVIs, enables algorithms with improved rates and simpler analyses.

Recent approaches to Φ\Phi-regret minimization have considered ever-increasing sets of transformations Φ\Phi and general convex action sets 𝒵\mathcal{Z} [13, 3, 66]. In all these applications, a recurring technical challenge is that GGM requires that the transformations ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi have fixed points in 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. And unfortunately, the set of functions that admit fixed points is not convex.

To circumvent the issue, [13] was the first to introduce intricate semiseparation techniques to operate on supersets of linear endomorphisms of the action set 𝒵\mathcal{Z} that admit fixed points in 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. Extensions of these techniques have been critical to enable the results of [3] and [66]. Given the sophistication of semi-separation, it should not come as a surprise that these more recent results come at the cost of extremely technically involved algorithms and undesirably high dependency on the dimensionality of the action set. A recent paper of [2] ameliorated the issue by showing that, depending on the goal, semiseparation can be replaced by response-based approachability [4], although the method is not known to be efficient for low-degree polynomial deviations, and the regret bounds require a (possibly non-polynomial-time) preprocessing of the strategy set 𝒵\mathcal{Z}.

In this section, we show that the EVI-based reduction from online learning to multicalibration (Theorem 4), combined with the reduction from multicalibration to Φ\Phi-regret minimization (Theorem 5), yields an EVI-based, forecasting-centric alternative to the otherwise fixed-point-based construction of [35] that overcomes many of the aforementioned shortcomings.

4.1 Improving Rates for Linear Swap Minimization

To fix ideas, consider the main problem studied by [13]: constructing a linear swap-regret minimizer for a well-bounded (Definition 3) convex compact set 𝒵⊆ℝd\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}, facing losses from a well-bounded convex compact set ℒ⊆ℝd\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}. For both sets, we assume efficient oracle access. In this setting, the set of transformations Φ\Phi is the set of all linear mappings from 𝒵\mathcal{Z} to 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, i.e., all linear endomorphisms of 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. We assume that the set of loss vectors ℒ\mathcal{L} has maximum Euclidean norm LL, each point in 𝒵\mathcal{Z} has maximum Euclidean norm BB, and that the geometry of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is such that the every linear endomorphism of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} has maximum spectral norm SS. We remark that the Fritz John’s theorem implies that any convex body admits a linear transformation ensuring that S=B=dS=B=d.

In this setting, the classical GGM approach to Φ\Phi-regret minimization would reduce to regret minimization over Φ\Phi. Unfortunately, the latter computational task is daunting, since testing membership in the set of endomorphisms is provably hard [13]. By instead taking a forecasting point of view, we can construct a no-linear-swap regret minimizer for Φ\Phi starting from any online forecaster for the convex loss set ℒ⊆ℝd\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} that is multicalibrated with respect to the class of tests

ℋΦ≔{(x,p)↦σ⁡(p)−ϕ⁡(σ⁡(p)):ϕ∈Φ},\mathcal{H}_{\Phi}\coloneqq\{(x,p)\mapsto\sigma(p)-\phi(\sigma(p)):\phi\in\Phi\},

where σ\sigma is the best-response function on 𝒵\mathcal{Z} (see Equation 4). Since the ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi are linear functions, each element of ℋΦ\mathcal{H}_{\Phi} is a linear function of σ⁡(p)\sigma(p). Hence, one way to multicalibrate with respect to ℋΦ\mathcal{H}_{\Phi} is to multicalibrate with respect to the ball of all linear functions

ℋ≔{(x,p)↦M​σ​(p):‖M‖F≤ρ},\mathcal{H}\coloneqq\{(x,p)\mapsto M\sigma(p):\|M\|_{F}\leq\rho\},

where we set the parameter ρ>0\rho>0 to be large enough. In particular, since we assumed that each linear endomorphism has maximum spectral norm SS, and ∥⋅∥F≤d∥⋅∥spectral\|\cdot\|_{F}\leq\sqrt{d}\|\cdot\|_{\text{spectral}}, it suffices to set ρ=d+d​S\rho=\sqrt{d}+\sqrt{d}S to ensure capturing all functions in ℋΦ\mathcal{H}_{\Phi}.

By leveraging Theorems 4 and 5, we can then reduce ℋ\mathcal{H}-multicalibration to online learning on ℋ\mathcal{H} with linear losses where we optimize over matrices {M∈ℝd×d:‖M‖F≤ρ}\{M\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}:\|M\|_{F}\leq\rho\}. Crucially, several standard no-regret algorithms can be applied off-the-shelf on the Frobenius ball. In particular, by invoking the standard analysis of online projected gradient descent, we obtain the following.

Proposition 4.

Let 𝒵,ℒ⊆ℝd\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be well-bounded convex bodies given via efficient oracle access. We let LL denote the maximum Euclidean norm of any vector in ℒ\mathcal{L}, BB denote the maximum Euclidean norm of any point in 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, and SS denote the maximum spectral (operator) norm of any linear endomorphism of 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. There exists a linear swap minimization algorithm for strategy set 𝒵\mathcal{Z} and loss set ℒ\mathcal{L} with polynomial-time iterations that guarantees 𝒪⁡(B​L​S​d​T)\mathcal{O}(BLS\sqrt{dT}) linear swap regret for any time horizon TT, no matter the sequence of losses ℓ1,…,ℓT∈ℒ\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{T}\in\mathcal{L}.

Proof.

We construct the ℋ\mathcal{H}-multicalibrated forecaster by instantiating Theorem 4 using projected gradient descent on {M∈ℝd×d:‖M‖F≤ρ}\{M\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}:\|M\|_{F}\leq\rho\}. At every time tt, the algorithm outputs a matrix MtM_{t} inducing the test p↦M​σ​(p)∈ℋp\mapsto M\sigma(p)\in\mathcal{H}, and incurs the linear loss

ft​(M)=−𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[(M​σ​(pt))⊤​(ℓt−pt)]=−⟨M,𝔼pt∼𝒟t​[(ℓt−pt)​σ​(pt)⊤]⟩F.\displaystyle f_{t}(M)=-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[(M\sigma(p_{t}))^{\top}(\ell_{t}-p_{t})\Big]=-\Big\langle M,\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\Big[(\ell_{t}-p_{t})\sigma(p_{t})^{\top}\Big]\Big\rangle_{F}.

Since pt,ℓt∈ℒp_{t},\ell_{t}\in\mathcal{L} and σ⁡(pt)∈𝒵\sigma(p_{t})\in\mathcal{Z}, the norm of the gradient of the loss function is therefore bounded by 𝒪⁡(L​B)\mathcal{O}(LB). Furthermore, by construction of ℋ\mathcal{H} the Frobenius norm of the domain is bounded above by d+d​S\sqrt{d}+\sqrt{d}S. Since S≥1S\geq 1 (the identity map is always an endomorphism of 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, and has unit spectral norm), the bound on the norm of the domain is therefore 𝒪⁡(d​S)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{d}S). Since the regret incurred by projected gradient descent scales as the norm of the domain, times the norm of the loss set, times T\sqrt{T}, we obtain a regret bound on ℋ\mathcal{H} of the order 𝒪⁡(B​L​S​d​T)\mathcal{O}(BLS\sqrt{dT}). By Theorem 4, if we solve the EVI problems to precision εt=t−2\varepsilon_{t}=t^{-2}, we get that EVIT≤𝒪⁡(1)\textrm{EVI}_{T}\leq\mathcal{O}(1) and for any linear endomorphism ϕ\phi:

RegretΦT​(ϕ)≤MC-ErrT​(hϕ)≤EVIT+RegretT​(hϕ)≤𝒪⁡(B​L​S​d​T).\displaystyle\textrm{Regret}^{T}_{\Phi}(\phi)\leq\textrm{MC-Err}_{T}(h_{\phi})\leq\textrm{EVI}_{T}+\textrm{Regret}_{T}(h_{\phi})\leq\mathcal{O}(BLS\sqrt{dT}).

We remark that the construction leads to polynomial-time iterates, in light of Fact 1 and the polynomial dimension of MM. ∎

If the set 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is already in John’s position and under the standard normalization assumption that |ℓ⊤​z|≤1|\ell^{\top}z|\leq 1 for all ℓ∈ℒ,z∈𝒵\ell\in\mathcal{L},z\in\mathcal{Z} (i.e., B=d,L=1,S=dB=d,L=1,S=d), this yields a rate of 𝒪⁡(d5/2​T)\mathcal{O}(d^{5/2}\sqrt{T}) which improves upon the rate 𝒪⁡(d4​T)\mathcal{O}(d^{4}\sqrt{T}) of [13].

However, the benefit of this forecasting approach to Φ\Phi-regret is not only its improved dependence on the dimension dd, but rather that it establishes a dramatically simpler algorithmic template. Indeed, while GGM-based approaches necessarily need to grapple with the complicated geometry of endomorphisms (expected fixed points of non-endomorphic maps need not exist, invalidating the GGM reduction), the multicalibration route is much more permissive: it is always easy to multicalibrate with respect to more tests. In our case, we promoted the set of tests from ℋΦ\mathcal{H}_{\Phi}, to the set of all linear multicalibration tests of sufficiently large norm, and the latter is no harder than performing online projected gradient descent on a Euclidean ball. We did not have to concern ourselves with whether the transformations in the enlarged set ℋ⊇ℋΦ\mathcal{H}\supseteq\mathcal{H}_{\Phi} admit fixed points in 𝒵\mathcal{Z}.

4.2 No-Φ\Phi-Regret with Respect to RKHS Deviations

Follow-up work to [13] has begun to explore Φ\Phi-regret minimization beyond linear deviations, including cases where the deviations are low-degree polynomials or endomorphisms given by a linear combination of a finite, polynomial number of nonlinear features [66].

In this section, we point out that the same approach outlined in Section 4.1 directly extends to these settings too. In fact, by multicalibrating over infinite sets of test functions using the techniques developed in Section 3.1, we can obtain, with no effort and for the first time, Φ\Phi-regret minimization algorithms in which Φ\Phi contains all transformations that lie in an RKHS ball (including RKHS with potentially infinitely many features, such as the Gaussian RKHS). This recovers low-degree polynomials as a special case.

Theorem 6.

Let 𝒵\mathcal{Z} be convex and compact with efficient oracle access, and let Φ\Phi be the subset of endomorphic functions ϕ:𝒳×𝒵→𝒵\phi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{Z} belonging to a vector-valued RKHS ℋ⊆{𝒳×𝒵→ℝd}\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\} with corresponding matrix-valued kernel Γ⁡((x,z),(x′,z′))\Gamma((x,z),(x^{\prime},z^{\prime})). Assume Γ\Gamma can be evaluated in polynomial time for any inputs and let ρ≔1+supϕ∈Φ‖ϕ‖ℋ\rho\coloneqq 1+\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\|\phi\|_{\mathcal{H}} scale additively with the maximum RKHS norm of any of the functions in Φ\Phi. Then, using Defensive Forecasting (Algorithm 3, Proposition 1) with the following kernel,

Γ′​((x,p),(x′,p′))=σ⁡(p)​σ​(p′)⊤+Γ⁡((x,σ⁡(p)),(x′,σ⁡(p′))),\displaystyle\Gamma^{\prime}((x,p),(x^{\prime},p^{\prime}))=\sigma(p)\sigma(p^{\prime})^{\top}+\Gamma((x,\sigma(p)),(x^{\prime},\sigma(p^{\prime}))), (15)

as the loss forecaster in the black-box reduction between multicalibration and Φ\Phi-regret minimization (Algorithm 2) produces distributions μt\mu_{t} over 𝒵\mathcal{Z} satisfying the following for any sequence {ℓt}t=1T\{\ell_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}:

supϕ∈Φ∑t=1T𝔼zt∼μt​[ℓt⊤​(zt−ϕ⁡(xt,zt))]≤𝒪⁡(ρ​∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​(pt−ℓt)⊤​Γ′​((xt,pt),(xt,pt))​(pt−ℓt)).\displaystyle\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{z_{t}\sim\mu_{t}}\Big[\ell_{t}^{\top}(z_{t}-\phi(x_{t},z_{t}))\Big]\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\rho\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}(p_{t}-\ell_{t})^{\top}\Gamma^{\prime}((x_{t},p_{t}),(x_{t},p_{t}))(p_{t}-\ell_{t})}\right).
Proof.

Since 𝒵\mathcal{Z} has an efficient linear optimization oracle, evaluations of the best response map σ:p↦arg​minz∈𝒵⁡p⊤​z\sigma:p\mapsto\argmin_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}p^{\top}z are also efficient. From Theorem 5, it suffices to construct an ℋΦ\mathcal{H}_{\Phi} multicalibrated forecaster for the loss set ℒ={ℓ∈ℝd:|ℓ⊤​z|≤1​∀z∈𝒵}\mathcal{L}=\{\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:|\ell^{\top}z|\leq 1~~\forall z\in\mathcal{Z}\}, where

ℋΦ={(x,p)↦σ⁡(p)−ϕ⁡(σ⁡(p)):ϕ∈Φ}.\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\Phi}=\{(x,p)\mapsto\sigma(p)-\phi(\sigma(p)):\phi\in\Phi\}. (16)

The crucial observation is that since every deviation ϕ\phi belongs to an RKHS with kernel Γ⁡((x,p),(x′,p′))\Gamma((x,p),(x^{\prime},p^{\prime})), then ϕ⁡(σ⁡(p))\phi(\sigma(p)) belongs to an RKHS with kernel Γ⁡((x,σ⁡(p)),(x′,σ⁡(p′)))\Gamma((x,\sigma(p)),(x^{\prime},\sigma(p^{\prime}))) and the functions σ⁡(p)−ϕ⁡(x,σ⁡(p))\sigma(p)-\phi(x,\sigma(p)) belong the RKHS corresponding to the kernel in Equation 15.

This makes use of the fact that if f1f_{1} is in the RKHS defined by kernel Γ1\Gamma_{1} and f2f_{2} is in the RKHS defined by Γ2\Gamma_{2}, then Γ1+Γ2\Gamma_{1}+\Gamma_{2} is a kernel that contains f1+f2f_{1}+f_{2}. Furthermore, the norm of f1+f2f_{1}+f_{2} in the new RKHS is at most the square root of the sum of the squared norms.

The functions σ⁡(p)\sigma(p) lie in the RKHS corresponding to the linear kernel σ⁡(p)​σ​(p′)⊤\sigma(p)\sigma(p^{\prime})^{\top} and have norm at most 1. Furthermore, ϕ⁡(x,σ⁡(p))\phi(x,\sigma(p)) lie in the RKHS corresponding to Γ⁡((x,σ⁡(p)),(x′,σ⁡(p′)))\Gamma((x,\sigma(p)),(x^{\prime},\sigma(p^{\prime}))) and have norm at most ρ\rho by our assumption on Γ\Gamma and Theorem 5.14 in [57]. Therefore, Proposition 1 guarantees that the multicalibration error of the forecaster with respect to the functions in Equation 16 is at most

𝒪⁡(ρ​∑t=1T𝔼pt∼𝒟t​(pt−ℓt)⊤​Γ′​((xt,pt),(xt,pt))​(pt−ℓt)).\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\left(\rho\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}(p_{t}-\ell_{t})^{\top}\Gamma^{\prime}((x_{t},p_{t}),(x_{t},p_{t}))(p_{t}-\ell_{t})}\right).

The bound on Φ\Phi-regret follows from our main result in Theorem 5. ∎

Note that this result is in fact stated for the stronger notion of contextual regret where the decision maker can observe features each round, and considers deviations of their actions that depend on such contexts. Furthermore, we state the result for general kernels Γ\Gamma to illustrate a tighter sequence-dependent bound. However, virtually all known kernels (polynomial, Gaussian, etc.) have ‖Γ⁡((x,p),(x,p))‖op\|\Gamma((x,p),(x,p))\|_{\mathrm{op}} bounded by a constant BB. In this case, we can replace the bound by one of the form 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}) where the 𝒪⁡(⋅)\mathcal{O}(\cdot) hides dependence on BB and the norms of ℓt\ell_{t}.
